chapters.title: The Mismatch, and the Claim
chapters.body:
Labelled data for a language task is made by people. Someone reads a pair of sentences and writes down whether the second follows from the first. That is slow, and it costs money, so the datasets stay small ([[labeled-data-scarcity]]).

Raw text has no such ceiling. There is far more of it than anyone could annotate.

The paper gathers a spread of tasks under one heading — entailment, question answering, sentence similarity, document classification — and calls the set [[natural-language-understanding]]. Each has its own dataset and its own idea of a correct answer. The standard treatment trains a network to predict the label directly from the input, which is [[generative-vs-discriminative-training|discriminative training]]. The scarce labels then have to pay for everything the network learns, down to how sentences are put together.

The alternative is to learn from raw text first, and spend the labels on the task alone. The paper says two things stood in the way of doing that. Nobody knew which unsupervised objective produced representations that transfer well ([[choice-of-pretraining-objective]]). And nobody agreed on how to move a learned representation into a target task once you had one ([[how-to-transfer-representations]]).

What is offered here is a [[two-stage-training-procedure]]. Train a language model on unlabelled text. Then keep those weights and go on training the same network on the labelled task.

The network is the [[transformer-gpt1|transformer]] of prior work, not a new design. Nothing is frozen, and no task-shaped module is bolted on top.

The claim is that this beats systems built by hand for each individual task. The paper reports new best published numbers on [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12|nine of the twelve datasets]] it measures, its largest margins being 8.9 points on commonsense story completion and 5.7 on exam-style reading comprehension.

[[theme-the-problem-and-the-open-questions|The problem and the two open questions]] have their own page.

chapters.title: Which Family This Joins
chapters.body:
Using unlabelled text to help a supervised task was already ordinary practice. So the related work section has one job: name the family, cut it into branches, and say which branch this is.

The family is [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]] — a large unlabelled corpus alongside a small labelled one. Its best-known members train one vector per word on raw text and reuse that table inside a task model ([[word-embedding-transfer]]). The paper grants that this works, then notes it carries word-level information only. Later work pushed upward to [[phrase-and-sentence-embeddings]], one vector for a longer span.

Cut the family a second way, by what the unlabelled data is allowed to change. One branch adds a second unsupervised loss beside the supervised one ([[auxiliary-training-objectives]]), so the training objective itself changes. The other leaves the objective alone and uses unlabelled data only to choose where optimization starts ([[unsupervised-pretraining]]). A cited result there says the benefit is not only easier optimization: the starting point also generalizes better ([[pretraining-as-regularization]]).

The paper sits in that second branch, and splits it once more.

[[feature-based-transfer]] freezes the pre-trained model and feeds its hidden states into a separate task network as extra inputs; [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] is the example named. The objection is [[per-task-parameter-cost]]. The task network is built fresh for every task, so each task pays for a substantial set of newly initialized parameters.

The line the paper calls closest to its own carries the weights themselves forward instead ([[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]]). [[semi-supervised-sequence-learning]] did this with a recurrent network for [[text-classification]], and [[ulmfit]] with a staged fine-tuning schedule for the same kind of task.

So the disagreement is not about the recipe. It is about the architecture and the reach. The paper argues a recurrent pre-trained model keeps its predictions local ([[lstm-short-range-limitation]]), and that it evaluates on far more than classification.

[[theme-where-this-sits-in-prior-work|The full map of branches]] goes deeper.

chapters.title: One Set of Weights, Used Twice
chapters.body:
The recipe in outline. Stage one, [[generative-pretraining]]: fit a language model to a large unlabelled corpus, and keep the weights rather than any text it generates. Stage two, [[supervised-fine-tuning]]: take those exact weights as the initialization and go on training them on a task's labelled examples.

That is all [[transfer-learning|the transfer]] amounts to here. No layer is frozen. The pre-trained model is not consulted from outside as a feature extractor — it becomes the task model.

Two consequences follow, and the paper leans on both.

First, the same stack is what gets fine-tuned every time. That is what it means by a [[task-agnostic-model]], and the comparison it wants is against [[task-specific-architectures]]: networks designed around one task's structure, which is what most of the published baselines are.

Second, the pre-training text need not resemble the task text. The paper states that the target tasks are not required to be in the same domain as the unlabelled corpus ([[domain-mismatch-tolerance]]). Books are the pre-training text; the evaluation includes science exams, news, image captions and Wikipedia.

That is an assumption stated, not a result shown. No matched-domain corpus is run as a control.

What remains to specify is what stage one optimizes, what network it optimizes, and what stage two does with the result. The next chapters take those in order.

[[theme-one-model-two-stages|The two-stage recipe]], and [[etheme-scarce-labels-borrowed-weights|the line from scarce labels to borrowed weights]].

chapters.title: Predicting the Next Token
chapters.body:
Stage one has no labels, so the training signal has to come out of the text itself. The paper takes the oldest one available: given the tokens so far, predict the one that comes next.

Written down, that is [[eq-lm-objective|Equation 1]]. Over an unlabelled corpus of tokens $\mathcal{U}$, maximize

$$L_1(\mathcal{U}) = \sum_i \log P(u_i \mid u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1};\Theta)$$

Read it position by position. At each $i$ the network sees the $k$ tokens before it and produces a distribution over the vocabulary. The number added into the sum is the log-probability it gave the token that actually appeared.

This is [[maximum-likelihood-training|maximum likelihood]] applied to text, and it is the whole of stage one. Every parameter the model has is set by pushing this single sum up ([[language-modeling-objective]]).

The network is a [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]]: the transformer block of prior work with the encoder half removed, leaving one stack that reads only its own past ([[decoder-only-stack]]).

That removal is load-bearing. The objective scores every position at once, and a position must not see the token it is being asked to predict. [[masked-self-attention]] enforces it — each position attends to itself and to earlier positions, never to later ones. Without the mask the loss would be trivial to drive down and would teach nothing.

[[eq-decoder-stack|Equation 2]] writes the network out in three lines. Embed the context tokens and add position vectors, giving $h_0 = UW_e + W_p$ ([[input-representation-h0]]). $W_e$ is the [[token-embedding-matrix]]; $W_p$ is a trained table with one vector per slot ([[learned-position-embeddings]]) rather than the fixed sinusoids of the original transformer. Push the result through $n$ identical blocks. Multiply the top layer by $W_e^{\mathsf{T}}$ and softmax ([[output-softmax-tied-embeddings]]), so the matrix that turns tokens into vectors also turns vectors back into token scores.

[[theme-stage-one-next-token-prediction|Stage one in full]], and [[etheme-the-next-token-machine|the loss and the network taken as one argument]].

chapters.title: The Corpus, the Model, the Run
chapters.body:
The objective says what to maximize. It does not say over what text, in what units, or with which optimizer.

The corpus is [[bookscorpus]]: over 7,000 unpublished books across genres. The stated reason for choosing it is not size. It is that a book keeps its sentences in their original order across paragraphs ([[long-range-contiguous-text]]).

The comparison makes the point. The [[one-billion-word-benchmark|1B Word Benchmark]] is about the same size, and is the corpus ELMo used, but it is shuffled sentence by sentence. Shuffling leaves the word statistics intact and destroys everything above the sentence.

That matters because of how much the model may look at. The context window $k$ is fixed at 512 tokens ([[context-window-512-tokens]]). 512 tokens is several paragraphs, so a prediction can condition on material from well before the current sentence — the [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|far-apart relations]] the paper wants learned. A window that wide only earns its cost if the text inside it is genuinely continuous.

Text becomes tokens in three steps ([[text-preprocessing-pipeline]]): clean the raw text, tokenize it, then cut the tokens into subword units with [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1|byte-pair encoding]]. BPE starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair. The count of merges is the single knob, set to [[bpe-merges-40000|40,000]] — enough that common words survive whole while rare ones break into pieces seen elsewhere.

The trained model is 12 blocks deep, with [[hidden-state-dimension-768|768-dimensional states]], [[twelve-attention-heads|12 attention heads]] and a [[position-wise-feedforward-3072|3072-dimensional]] inner feed-forward layer ([[model-specification]]). The numbers are related: 768 split across 12 heads leaves each head a 64-dimensional subspace, and 3072 is four times 768. [[twelve-layer-depth|The depth of 12]] is also what makes a later experiment possible — you can transfer 0 through 12 layers and watch what happens. [[gelu|GELU]] stands in for ReLU as the activation.

The run uses [[adam-optimizer-gpt1|Adam]] at a peak rate of 2.5e-4, [[linear-warmup|raised from zero over 2000 updates]] then [[cosine-annealing|annealed back to zero on a cosine curve]], for [[pretraining-schedule|100 passes]] over minibatches of 64 sequences ([[pre-training-optimization]]). Dropout in three places and a [[decoupled-weight-decay]] do the regularizing ([[regularization-setup]]).

The reported outcome is one number: [[token-level-perplexity|18.4]] token-level perplexity on the corpus. It says the model fit the books. It says nothing yet about any task.

[[theme-corpus-tokens-and-training-setup|Corpus, tokens and setup]]; [[etheme-the-long-range-bet|the bet on long stretches of text]].

chapters.title: From Language Model to Classifier
chapters.body:
Stage two has to turn a next-token predictor into a label predictor, the same way for every task.

The labelled data is [[labeled-dataset-c|$\mathcal{C}$]]: each instance is a token sequence $x_1,\dots,x_m$ paired with one label $y$.

Run the sequence through the pre-trained stack. Take the final block's activation at the last token ([[final-token-activation]]) — one vector, which has attended over everything before it. Multiply it by one added matrix $W_y$ ([[linear-output-layer-wy]]) and softmax. That is [[eq-task-head|Equation 3]], and it is the entire task-specific classifier.

The loss is then ordinary supervised likelihood: sum $\log P(y \mid x_1,\dots,x_m)$ over the labelled data ([[eq-supervised-objective|Equation 4]], [[supervised-objective-l2|$L_2$]]).

The paper does not stop there. It keeps the language modelling loss running during fine-tuning, computed on the labelled task data, and adds it in ([[auxiliary-lm-objective]]):

$$L_3(\mathcal{C}) = L_2(\mathcal{C}) + \lambda\, L_1(\mathcal{C})$$

with [[auxiliary-objective-weight|$\lambda = 0.5$]] ([[eq-combined-objective]]). The stated reasons are better generalization and faster convergence.

Notice what has happened. This is the auxiliary-objective idea the related work described as a rival branch, used here on top of pre-training instead of in place of it. The last chapter reports what happens when it is taken away, and the answer is not uniform.

Fine-tuning is short. Most tasks use a learning rate of 6.25e-5, about four times smaller than pre-training's peak, at batch size 32 ([[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch]]). The rate warms up over the first 0.2% of updates and then decays linearly to zero ([[fine-tuning-lr-schedule]]). [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|Three passes]] over a task's training set sufficed for most datasets, with [[classifier-dropout|dropout 0.1]] on the added head and everything else inherited from stage one ([[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]]).

[[theme-stage-two-fine-tuning-and-input-shapes|Stage two in full]].

chapters.title: One Sequence Per Task
chapters.body:
A decoder reads one ordered run of tokens. Several of these tasks do not hand over one run of tokens. Entailment gives an ordered sentence pair; reading comprehension gives a document, a question and a list of candidate answers ([[structured-inputs]]).

There are two places to absorb that difference. Prior work absorbs it in the architecture, building a module shaped like the task and stacking it on the transferred representation. The paper's objection is that this puts per-task design back in, and that the new module gets nothing from pre-training.

So it absorbs the difference in the input ([[task-specific-input-transformations]]). Each structured input is walked into a single sequence ([[traversal-style-approach]]), bracketed by a randomly initialized start and end token ([[start-and-end-tokens]]) and split by a `$` [[delimiter-token|delimiter]].

Entailment becomes premise, delimiter, hypothesis, read as one sequence ([[entailment-input-transformation]]).

Similarity has no natural order between its two sentences. So both orderings are built and run through the stack separately, and the two final activations are added element-wise before the linear layer ([[similarity-input-transformation]]).

Question answering builds one sequence per candidate — document, question, delimiter, that answer. Each is scored on its own, and the scores are softmaxed across candidates ([[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]]).

[[fig-1]] draws all four shapes beside the block they feed.

This is what keeps the parameter count small. The only weights a new task adds are $W_y$ and embeddings for the delimiter tokens ([[minimal-extra-parameters]]), which is the paper's direct answer to the per-task cost it charged against [[feature-based-transfer|feature-based transfer]].

It is also what makes the evaluation menu possible: [[evaluation-task-families|four families across twelve datasets]], listed in [[table-1]], several drawn from the [[glue-benchmark|GLUE]] bundle.

[[etheme-one-stack-any-input-shape|One stack, any input shape]].

chapters.title: The Scoreboard
chapters.body:
Gains are reported as [[absolute-improvement|differences in percentage points]] against the previous best published number, not as relative error reduction. On the other side are mostly biLSTMs built for the individual task, some with attention, some with ELMo features, some ensembles ([[baseline-comparisons]]).

[[natural-language-inference]] asks for a judgement on a premise and hypothesis: entailment, contradiction or neutral. Five datasets, in [[table-2]]. The fine-tuned model leads on four — 1.5 points on [[multinli|MultiNLI]], 5 on [[scitail|SciTail]], 5.8 on [[qnli|QNLI]], and 0.6 on [[snli|SNLI]], the largest set at roughly 550k training pairs.

It loses the fifth. [[rte|RTE]] has 2,490 training examples, and the model reaches 56% against 61.7% from a multi-task biLSTM. The paper's reading is that its approach would probably also benefit from multi-task training, and it says it has not tried.

[[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning|Reading and commonsense reasoning]] give the widest margins ([[table-3]]). On [[race-dataset|RACE]], middle- and high-school exam passages with questions, the gain is 5.7 points overall. On the [[story-cloze-test|Story Cloze Test]], choosing the right ending to a short story from two options, it is 8.9. Both reward conditioning on a long passage, which is what the corpus and the 512-token window were chosen for.

[[semantic-similarity]] and [[text-classification]] fill out [[table-4]]. [[qqp|Quora Question Pairs]] gains 4.2 points over a single-task biLSTM with ELMo and attention. [[sts-b|STS-B]], the smallest set in the evaluation at about 5.7k examples, gains 1 point. On [[cola|CoLA]], expert judgements of whether a sentence is grammatical, the score is 45.4 against a previous best of 35.0 — a jump of 10.4 points, the widest gap on the board. On [[sst-2|SST-2]] sentiment the model reaches 91.3%, which the paper calls competitive rather than best. The overall GLUE score is 72.8 against a previous 68.9.

Counted up: new best published results on [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12|nine of twelve datasets]], over training sets spanning two orders of magnitude in size.

[[theme-what-the-twelve-datasets-show|Dataset by dataset]]; [[etheme-the-scoreboard-and-its-gaps|the scoreboard and its gaps]].

chapters.title: Which Parts Do the Work, and What Is Left Open
chapters.body:
The results say the recipe works. They do not say which part of it works. The analysis section asks three times.

First, how much of the stack is worth carrying. Fine-tune with the embeddings alone transferred, then with one block, then two, up to all twelve, and plot dev accuracy ([[layers-transferred]], left panel of [[fig-2]]). Accuracy climbs with each added layer, up to 9 points on MultiNLI at full transfer. Nothing saturates early. The reading offered is that every layer holds something a target task can use, so moving embeddings alone leaves most of the value behind.

Second, what the model can already do with no fine-tuning at all ([[zero-shot-behaviors]]). A generative model does not emit labels, so each task is turned into a scoring problem. Three of four heuristics use the same device — the mean log-probability the model assigns a candidate string ([[average-token-log-probability-scoring]]). Threshold that score for grammatical acceptability ([[cola-zero-shot-heuristic]]); pick the highest-scoring answer given document and question ([[race-zero-shot-heuristic]]); or substitute each candidate referent for a pronoun and keep the reading that scores better ([[dprd-winograd-heuristic]]). Sentiment is done differently: append the token *very*, restrict the output to *positive* and *negative*, take the higher ([[sst2-zero-shot-heuristic]]).

Tracked across pre-training, all four rise steadily and stay stable. The paper reads that as pre-training picking up task-relevant behaviour on its way to better next-token prediction. An LSTM run the same way is noisier, offered as support for [[transformer-inductive-bias|the transformer's more structured memory helping transfer]] — a hypothesis resting on one comparison.

Third, the removals ([[ablation-studies]], [[table-5]]). Training the same transformer straight on the labelled tasks with no pre-training costs 14.8 average points and hurts on every task ([[ablation-no-pretraining]]). That is the strongest single number in the paper. Swapping the transformer for a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM costs 5.6, and the LSTM wins on exactly one dataset, [[mrpc|MRPC]] ([[ablation-lstm-substitution]]).

The third removal is the awkward one. Dropping the auxiliary language modelling loss during fine-tuning does not simply degrade the model — it helps on some datasets and hurts on others ([[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]]). The paper reads the pattern as larger datasets benefiting from the loss and smaller ones not.

### What is established, and what is not

Pre-training on unlabelled books and then fine-tuning the same weights beats task-built systems on nine of twelve datasets, and the no-pre-training row says most of that comes from stage one. Depth keeps paying across all twelve layers on the two datasets swept. Those are the results that hold their weight.

The gaps are visible in the paper's own numbers. RTE, the smallest inference set, is a loss, and the explanation given — that multi-task training would help — is not tested here. The auxiliary loss is part of the recipe but its own ablation shows it helping only on the larger sets, a trend drawn from twelve points with no repeated runs. Every number is a single run against a published best, with no variance reported on either side. And the GLUE figure does not sit still: the results section compares 72.8 against 68.9, a difference of 3.9, while the introduction's headline for GLUE is 5.5.

The conclusion also reaches past the experiments, saying the model acquires [[world-knowledge|significant world knowledge]] from predicting text. Nothing in the evaluation separates knowledge from the reading ability these tasks also reward.

[[theme-taking-the-recipe-apart|The three diagnostics]], [[etheme-watching-pre-training-work|what pre-training is doing]], and [[etheme-two-losses-and-three-removals|the two losses and the three removals]].

n-the-mismatch.title: The Mismatch, and the Claim
n-the-mismatch.intro: The parent gave the problem and the promise. This level reads the introduction as an argument: two separate reasons for wanting raw text, two questions the paper says were blocking anyone from using it, the preconditions the recipe quietly assumes, the single sentence offered in defence of the architecture, and what the headline claim does and does not cover.

chapters.title: Two Arguments, Not One
chapters.body:
The parent gave one reason to want raw text. The introduction gives two, and they are not the same reason.

The first is about coverage. Most deep learning methods need substantial hand-labelled data, and that requirement rules them out entirely in domains where annotation is thin ([[labeled-data-scarcity]]). The argument here is that supervised learning is unavailable, not that it is weak.

The second argument is a different shape. The paper says that even where considerable supervision is available, learning good representations without labels still gives a real gain.

Scarcity plays no part in that claim. It says unsupervised learning finds structure that training on a task's own labels would not find, however many labels you had ([[generative-vs-discriminative-training]]).

That second claim needs evidence, and the introduction names some. Pre-trained word embeddings are already in wide use across [[natural-language-understanding|language understanding tasks]], and the paper calls this the most compelling evidence so far that unsupervised representations help ([[word-embedding-transfer]]).

Then it names the limit of that evidence. It is word-level. One vector per word type, learned once, reused everywhere.

The stated difficulty is getting above that line — using more than word-level information from unlabelled text ([[phrase-and-sentence-embeddings]]).

So the question the paper opens on is not whether unlabelled text helps at all. Inside [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp|semi-supervised NLP]] that is treated as already answered at the word level. What is open is whether anything larger than a word transfers.

chapters.title: What the Two Open Questions Were Made Of
chapters.body:
The parent said two things stood in the way. The introduction says what each one consisted of.

The first is the objective ([[choice-of-pretraining-objective]]). The problem was not a shortage of candidates. The paper names three recent lines of work: predicting the next token ([[language-modeling-objective|language modelling]]), translating between languages, and judging discourse coherence.

Each one, the paper says, outperforms the others on different tasks. That is the actual state of the evidence — not a ranking, a scatter.

The footnote attached to that sentence is not a citation. It is a link to a public leaderboard ([[glue-benchmark]]), which is a fair signal of how live the question still was.

Note what the introduction does not do. It picks language modelling and offers no argument here for the choice. The argument is deferred to measurements later in the paper.

The second question is transfer ([[how-to-transfer-representations]]). Suppose you already hold a pre-trained representation. Existing practice, as the paper describes it, mixed three kinds of machinery: changes to the model architecture shaped around the target task ([[task-specific-architectures]]), intricate learning schemes, and extra unsupervised loss terms carried alongside the supervised one ([[auxiliary-training-objectives]]). A further option was to freeze the pre-trained model and pipe its hidden states into a separate task network as features ([[feature-based-transfer]]).

So "no consensus" means something specific. Several mechanisms were in use at once, each traced to a different paper, with no agreement about which was carrying the result.

The paper's own diagnosis closes the paragraph. These two uncertainties are why effective semi-supervised approaches for language had been difficult to build.

chapters.title: What the Recipe Assumes It Has
chapters.body:
The [[two-stage-training-procedure|two-stage procedure]] has preconditions, and the introduction states them before describing the method.

One: access to a large corpus of unlabelled text — here, a collection of books ([[bookscorpus]]). Two: several datasets of manually annotated training examples, which the paper calls the target tasks ([[labeled-dataset-c]]).

Then comes one sentence that is easy to read past. The setup does not require the target tasks to be in the same domain as the unlabelled corpus ([[domain-mismatch-tolerance]]).

It is worth sitting with that. If domain match were required, every target task would need its own matched pile of raw text.

The scarcity problem would then return one level up, in a different currency — unlabelled text is abundant in general, but not necessarily abundant and on-topic. The point of pre-training once is that the same weights ([[transfer-learning]]) serve tasks whose text looks nothing like the corpus.

The paper asserts this rather than testing it directly. The evidence is indirect: one corpus of books, then [[evaluation-task-families|twelve datasets]] drawn from image captions, news wire, Wikipedia, science exams and a question forum.

The goal is stated as a universal representation that transfers with little adaptation. Two separate commitments are packed into that phrase.

Universal means one representation for all the tasks, rather than one per task ([[task-agnostic-model]]).

Little adaptation means the cost of taking on a new task should be small. Later in the paper that becomes a countable quantity: how many freshly initialized parameters each new task adds ([[minimal-extra-parameters]]).

chapters.title: The One Sentence on the Architecture
chapters.body:
The parent said the network is prior work's transformer, not a new design. The introduction does give a reason for that choice, and the reason is one sentence long.

The [[transformer-gpt1|transformer]] is said to provide a more structured memory for handling long-term dependencies in text, compared with alternatives like recurrent networks ([[lstm-gpt1]]).

Unpack that. A recurrent network carries everything it has read in a single hidden state of fixed size, rewritten at every step. Older material survives only to the extent that it survived each rewrite.

Self-attention instead keeps every earlier position addressable. A prediction can reach back to a specific token directly, without that token having to have been preserved through hundreds of updates.

What the paper wants from that reach is [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|dependencies spanning many tokens]] — a pronoun and the name it stands for several sentences earlier, or an exam question and the one line of the passage that answers it.

Then the introduction takes a further step. It says this structured memory results in robust transfer performance across diverse tasks ([[transformer-inductive-bias]]).

At this point in the paper that is an assertion. The citations offered are for the transformer's strength on machine translation, document generation and syntactic parsing. None of those are transfer results.

The evidence comes much later, and as a removal: hold the whole recipe fixed, swap in a single-layer LSTM, and the average score falls by 5.6 points ([[ablation-lstm-substitution]]).

The same paragraph also commits early to handling [[structured-inputs|multi-part inputs]] by walking them into one contiguous sequence ([[traversal-style-approach]]), rather than by building task-shaped modules ([[task-specific-input-transformations]]).

chapters.title: The Claim, and What It Leaves Out
chapters.body:
The parent gave the headline: new best published results on [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12|nine of twelve datasets]]. Read the sentence closely and three things sharpen.

First, the comparison class. The model is said to outperform discriminatively trained models that use architectures specifically crafted for each task ([[baseline-comparisons]]). The claim is staked against hand-built task systems. It is not a claim about beating other pre-trained models.

Second, the spread. Four families are named up front: [[natural-language-inference|inference]], [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning|question answering]], [[semantic-similarity|semantic similarity]] and [[text-classification|text classification]], covering [[table-1|twelve datasets]] between them. Breadth is part of the claim itself, since a single model that only worked on one family would settle nothing.

Third, how gains are counted. The introduction reports two figures the parent had no room for: 1.5 points on [[multinli|MultiNLI]] and 5.5 on the GLUE multi-task benchmark, beside 8.9 on the [[story-cloze-test|Story Cloze Test]] and 5.7 on [[race-dataset|RACE]].

These are absolute improvements ([[absolute-improvement]]). A gain of 8.9 means the accuracy figure moved 8.9 percentage points.

It does not mean errors fell by 8.9 percent. That relative figure would be the larger-sounding one on any task already scoring well, and the paper does not use it.

Now what the claim leaves out. Nine of twelve means three datasets where the previous best still stands, and the introduction does not name them.

One further piece of evidence is promised here. The paper says it also analysed [[zero-shot-behaviors|zero-shot behaviours]] across four settings, offered as a sign that pre-training alone leaves useful linguistic knowledge behind before any label is seen.

n-which-family-this-joins.title: Which Family This Joins
n-which-family-this-joins.intro: The parent named the branches. This level says what each branch actually does to a model — which parameters move, which stay frozen, which loss terms are summed — and checks how much of the paper's own placement is argument and how much is measurement.

chapters.title: What a Word Table Can Carry
chapters.body:
The oldest members of [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]] learned nothing at all. They computed word-level and phrase-level statistics over the unlabelled corpus — counts, co-occurrence figures — and handed those to a supervised model as extra input features.

Learned vectors came later. [[word-embedding-transfer]] trains one vector per vocabulary entry on raw text, then drops that table into a task model.

The mechanism is a lookup. Each word type owns one row. The row returned for a word is the same row every time that word appears, whatever sentence it appears in.

So the unlabelled corpus contributes a fixed quantity per word, settled before the task model sees anything. The tasks this was shown on match that granularity: sequence labelling, and [[text-classification]].

[[phrase-and-sentence-embeddings]] push the unit upward. One vector now stands for a whole phrase or sentence, trained on unlabelled text, then used as a feature for the target task. The vector is longer-range, but it is still a frozen quantity passed to a separately built network.

The paper's own model contains a table of exactly the first kind. [[token-embedding-matrix]] $W_e$ maps each token to a dense vector, and [[input-representation-h0]] adds position vectors to it: $h_0 = UW_e + W_p$.

That is layer zero. Twelve blocks sit above it, and [[final-token-activation]] at any position depends on every preceding token in the window.

So the thing carried across is not the table. It is the stack that reads the table — which is what lets a [[natural-language-understanding]] task see [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]] rather than a bag of per-word constants.

chapters.title: Change the Loss, or Change the Starting Point
chapters.body:
The second cut is about which part of training the unlabelled data touches.

[[auxiliary-training-objectives]] touch the loss. There is one training run, and the objective is a sum: the supervised term plus an unsupervised term computed on raw text. Gradients from both flow into the same shared weights at the same time.

The cited instances are concrete. Collobert and Weston attached a spread of auxiliary NLP tasks — part-of-speech tagging, chunking, named entity recognition, language modelling — to improve semantic role labelling. Rei added a single language modelling term beside a sequence labelling objective and reported gains.

[[unsupervised-pretraining]] leaves the objective alone. The supervised loss is exactly what it would have been; only the initial value of the weights differs.

That is a clean distinction, and the paper does not sit cleanly on one side of it.

[[supervised-fine-tuning]] here keeps a language modelling term running during stage two. [[auxiliary-lm-objective]] is written as $L_3(C) = L_2(C) + \lambda\, L_1(C)$, and [[eq-combined-objective]] is the paper's Equation 5. [[auxiliary-objective-weight]] is fixed at $\lambda = 0.5$.

By the branch definition, the paper is doing both things.

Its defence is a claim about magnitude, not category: pre-training already learns the linguistic aspects the auxiliary term would supply, so the term is a top-up rather than the engine.

[[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] is where that claim is cashed. In [[table-5]] the auxiliary term helps the larger datasets and hurts the smaller ones, and its effect is by far the smallest of the three removals tested.

chapters.title: A Technique Borrowed From Elsewhere
chapters.body:
The branch the paper joins did not start in NLP.

The early citations are image classification and regression. Unsupervised pre-training there was a way to get a deep network to train at all, by putting the weights somewhere reasonable before the supervised gradient arrived.

Then came a sharper finding. [[pretraining-as-regularization]] reports that the benefit is not only that optimization gets easier — the initialization also lands the network somewhere that generalizes better on held-out data.

That matters for how the paper reads its own results. If pre-training were only an optimization aid, its value would shrink as labelled data grew and optimization stopped being the binding constraint. The regularization reading says otherwise.

The paper cites this result. It does not re-run it.

More recent applications named are image classification again, speech recognition, entity disambiguation and machine translation. So the technique arrives already established across domains, and what is specific here is the domain and the choice of objective.

One consequence is stated as an assumption rather than tested directly. [[domain-mismatch-tolerance]] holds that the unlabelled corpus need not match the target domain, which is what permits books to initialize models scored on news sentences, Quora questions and science exams.

The paper's own measurement of what initialization is worth comes from [[ablation-no-pretraining]] in [[ablation-studies]]: the same transformer, the same [[two-stage-training-procedure]] minus stage one, trained straight on the supervised tasks, loses 14.8% across the board.

That number isolates [[transfer-learning]] cleanly, because architecture and fine-tuning objective are held fixed and only [[generative-pretraining]] is removed.

chapters.title: Freeze the Model, or Carry Its Weights
chapters.body:
Inside the initialization branch, the split is over what happens to the pre-trained weights once the target task arrives.

[[feature-based-transfer]] keeps them still. A pre-trained language or translation model is run over the task input, hidden states are read out of it, and those states are fed to a separate supervised network as extra features. No gradient from the task updates the pre-trained model.

[[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations]] is the instance named. Its features come from a pre-trained bidirectional language model, and they are consumed by a task network that is still designed and initialized per task.

That network is the cost. [[per-task-parameter-cost]] is the paper's objection: each new target task brings a substantial set of freshly initialized parameters, trained from scratch on that task's small labelled set.

The paper gives no count for this. The argument stays qualitative on the other side.

On its own side the arithmetic is short. [[minimal-extra-parameters]] amounts to [[linear-output-layer-wy]], a matrix from a 768-dimensional activation to however many classes the task has, plus embedding rows for the [[delimiter-token]] and the bracketing symbols. For a three-way inference task that is a few thousand new weights against a twelve-layer stack inherited whole.

Everything else is [[task-agnostic-model]]: one architecture, pre-trained once, not redesigned for anything — against [[task-specific-architectures]] built around each task's shape.

The divergence reaches the data as well. [[one-billion-word-benchmark]], the corpus behind the feature-based comparison, is about the same size as [[bookscorpus]] but shuffled at the sentence level, which removes the [[long-range-contiguous-text]] this paper says its corpus was chosen for.

chapters.title: The Closest Line, and What It Is Missing
chapters.body:
[[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]] is the line the paper calls closest to its own, and the closeness is real: pre-train with a language modelling objective, then fine-tune the whole network with supervision.

[[semi-supervised-sequence-learning]] did this with a recurrent network, pre-trained by language modelling or by autoencoding, then fine-tuned for [[text-classification]]. [[ulmfit]] pre-trained an LSTM language model and fine-tuned it on a staged schedule, again for classification.

The recipe is therefore not what is being claimed.

Two differences are claimed instead. [[lstm-short-range-limitation]] is the first: the paper argues a recurrent pre-trained model restricts its prediction ability to a short range, so however much linguistic information the pre-training phase captures, only nearby structure survives the transfer.

In the related work section this is asserted, with a forward pointer to the experiments. Nothing is measured there.

What arrives later is indirect but real. [[ablation-lstm-substitution]] swaps in a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM inside the same framework and loses 5.6 average points, winning on exactly one dataset, [[mrpc]]. [[layers-transferred]] in [[fig-2]] shows each transferred block adding accuracy, up to 9% on MultiNLI. [[transformer-inductive-bias]] rests on the LSTM showing higher variance in zero-shot scores.

None of that measures range directly. Range is inferred from an averaged score gap, supported by a [[context-window-512-tokens]] over contiguous book text.

The second difference needs no inference. The predecessors were evaluated on text classification; [[evaluation-task-families]] here spans inference, paraphrase detection and story completion across the twelve datasets of [[table-1]].

n-one-set-of-weights-used-twice.title: One Set of Weights, Used Twice
n-one-set-of-weights-used-twice.intro: The parent gave the recipe's shape. This level takes it apart at the level of parameters: what actually crosses from stage one into stage two, what is added, what fine-tuning everything costs, where the per-task work went once it left the architecture, and how much weight the domain assumption is carrying.

chapters.title: What Crosses the Boundary
chapters.body:
Fine-tuning here begins by loading a file of numbers. What sits in that file is the entire product of [[generative-pretraining|stage one]]: the [[token-embedding-matrix]], the position embeddings, and every weight in every block of the stack.

[[supervised-fine-tuning|Stage two]] does not wrap that file in anything. It sets the network's parameters to those values and carries on running gradient descent, now against a different loss. That is the whole of [[transfer-learning|the transfer]] in this [[two-stage-training-procedure|two-stage recipe]].

Which makes the interesting question an accounting one. How many parameters does a new task need that stage one did not already supply?

The paper's answer is two kinds, and it states them as a total ([[minimal-extra-parameters]]).

The first is the output layer [[linear-output-layer-wy|$W_y$]]. It maps the 768-dimensional activation at the last token to one score per label, so for a three-way entailment decision it is $768 \times 3$ numbers ([[eq-task-head]]).

The second is an embedding for each [[delimiter-token|delimiter symbol]] the rewritten inputs introduce, because those symbols carry no meaning learned during pre-training. Everything else is inherited.

Set that against the alternative the paper is arguing with. In [[feature-based-transfer]], the pre-trained model is frozen and run only to produce hidden states, which are handed to a separate supervised network as extra input features; [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] is the best-known instance. That separate network is designed and initialized for each task, so its full parameter count is a per-task cost.

The paper turns this into its comparison metric, [[per-task-parameter-cost]], and says such approaches involve a substantial number of new parameters for each separate target task.

Note what form that comparison takes. It is asserted, not counted: no parameter totals for either side appear anywhere in the paper.

chapters.title: The Price of Not Freezing
chapters.body:
If no layer is frozen, every weight in the twelve blocks is a free variable while the task loss is being minimized. Two consequences follow that the paper does not dwell on.

The first is bookkeeping. Fine-tuning ends with a full, separately modified copy of the [[model-specification|12-layer, 768-dimensional stack]] for each dataset, so twelve datasets means twelve models on disk.

A frozen pre-trained model with small task heads would keep one copy and add little per task. The paper's accounting counts freshly initialized parameters, where it wins; the storage accounting runs the other way, and is not reported.

The second is that gradients from a small labelled set can move those weights anywhere, including away from whatever made them worth transferring. Nothing in the framework prevents that.

The paper does not measure it either. It cites the older finding that [[unsupervised-pretraining|unsupervised pre-training]] acts as [[pretraining-as-regularization|a regularizer]] rather than only an optimization aid, which is a claim that the starting point keeps mattering — but that is a citation, not a measurement made here.

Two of its own choices bear on the risk without being presented as remedies for it. Fine-tuning runs at a learning rate well below the pre-training peak, for three passes over the task data ([[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]]). And the language modelling loss keeps being optimized during stage two ([[auxiliary-lm-objective]]), which the paper justifies by generalization and convergence speed, not by drift.

What the paper does supply is evidence that carrying the weights across is worth doing at all: one row of [[table-5]] retrains the same architecture with [[ablation-no-pretraining|no pre-training]], and a sweep in [[layers-transferred]] carries only part of the stack. Both live in a later chapter.

chapters.title: Where the Task-Specific Work Went
chapters.body:
The tasks in this evaluation are not the same shape. A sentiment example is one sentence; an entailment example is an ordered pair; a reading comprehension example is a document, a question and several candidate answers.

Something has to absorb that difference. It does not vanish because a model is called general.

In the systems the paper measures against, the architecture absorbs it. Those are [[task-specific-architectures]]: [[baseline-comparisons|mostly biLSTM]] networks with attention arranged around one task's structure, sometimes ensembled, which is what most published numbers on these datasets came from at the time.

Here the input absorbs it. [[structured-inputs]] are walked into a single ordered token sequence, a [[traversal-style-approach]], so the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder|same stack]] can read them unchanged ([[fig-1]], [[task-specific-input-transformations]]).

So [[task-agnostic-model|task-agnostic]] is a claim about the network, not about the pipeline. Per-task work still exists. It has moved from choosing layers to choosing a token order and a set of separator symbols.

The abstract is more careful than the shorthand suggests: it says task-aware input transformations, used to achieve transfer while requiring minimal changes to the model architecture.

And for two task families the per-task decision reaches slightly past the token string. [[similarity-input-transformation|Similarity]] runs both sentence orderings through the stack and adds the two final activations. [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation|Multiple choice]] runs one sequence per candidate answer and normalizes the scores across them.

Those are choices about how many forward passes to make and how to combine them. The stack itself is untouched, but the claim of no task-specific structure is doing slightly less work than it first appears.

chapters.title: Books In, Science Exams Out
chapters.body:
The [[domain-mismatch-tolerance|domain assumption]] appears once, in the introduction, as a single sentence about the setup: the target tasks are not required to be in the same domain as the unlabelled corpus.

It is worth seeing how wide the gap actually is. [[bookscorpus]] is over 7,000 unpublished books, in genres the paper lists as adventure, fantasy and romance.

Now the other end. [[snli]] is written over image captions. [[qnli]] is built from Wikipedia. [[scitail]] comes from science exam questions. [[rte]] and [[mrpc]] come from news. [[race-dataset]] is English exam passages set for Chinese students.

None of those reads like a work of fiction. The assumption is carrying every one of these datasets.

What would test it is a second pre-training run on a matched corpus, scored the same way. No such run is reported, so the assumption stays an assumption.

The corpus argument the paper does make runs on a different axis entirely. It names the [[one-billion-word-benchmark]] as the rejected alternative and argues from [[long-range-contiguous-text|contiguity]], not from subject matter — and even that comparison is made by argument rather than by training on both.

There is weak support in the results. The same weights do well across captions, news, Wikipedia and exam text, which is at least consistent with domain mattering little, though nothing here isolates domain as the variable.

One case is worth flagging. RTE is the single inference dataset where the paper does not take the best published number, and it reads that as a small-data effect at 2,490 training examples. RTE is also news text. The paper's reading may be right, but a domain reading is available and is not ruled out.

The conclusion goes further still, claiming the books leave the model with [[world-knowledge|world knowledge]] that transfers. That is an interpretation of the gains, not a separate measurement.

n-predicting-the-next-token.title: Predicting the Next Token
n-predicting-the-next-token.intro: The parent gave the loss and named the network. This level reads both at working scale: what one 512-token sequence actually buys in scored predictions, what the mask does inside a single attention head, what each line of Equation 2 commits the model to, and how large the stack that results is.

chapters.title: Reading the Sum as Work Done
chapters.body:
$k$ is a number, and the paper fixes it. [[eq-lm-objective|Equation 1]] writes the context as $u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1}$, and the trained model reads contiguous sequences of 512 tokens ([[context-window-512-tokens]]). A prediction can therefore condition on up to 511 tokens of preceding text.

That is paragraphs, not words. A pronoun and the name it stands for can sit several sentences apart, and a window this wide holds both at once ([[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]]).

Now read the sum as work rather than as notation. Take one sequence of 512 tokens. Every position after the first contributes a term to $L_1$, so a single sequence yields on the order of 511 scored predictions.

Each token in it plays two roles. Once it is the target, at its own position. Up to 511 times it is context, for the positions that come after it.

Nothing was annotated to arrange this. The target at position $i$ is the token already sitting at position $i$, so the label is the data shifted by one ([[generative-pretraining]]).

The terms are log-probabilities, so each is at most zero. A model that puts probability $0.5$ on the token that appeared contributes about $-0.69$; at $0.05$ it contributes about $-3.0$; at $0.9$, about $-0.11$. Driving the sum up means moving probability mass onto the tokens that actually occurred, and stage one applies no other pressure ([[maximum-likelihood-training]], [[language-modeling-objective]]).

The paper says these parameters are trained with stochastic gradient descent, and says no more than that here. They are the same parameters the second stage will start from ([[two-stage-training-procedure]]).

chapters.title: The Mask, and What the Missing Encoder Costs
chapters.body:
Inside one attention head the model forms a score for every ordered pair of positions: the query at $i$ against the key at $j$. [[masked-self-attention]] intervenes before the softmax over those scores. Every entry with $j > i$ is set to $-\infty$, so its weight after the softmax is exactly zero.

The output at position $i$ is then a mixture of values drawn from positions $1$ through $i$ and nothing else.

That property composes. If each layer is causal, a stack of them is causal, so a state at the top of the blocks still depends on no token after its own ([[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]]).

This is what makes scoring every position in one pass legitimate. Without the mask you would need a separate forward pass per position, each with the future cut away. With it, one pass over a 512-token sequence produces every term of the sum, and no term has seen its own answer.

The encoder is dropped for a separate reason. In the architecture this builds on ([[transformer-gpt1]]) a decoder block carries three sublayers, the middle one attending to an encoder's output. Pre-training has no source sequence and no target sequence, only one running stream of text, so that sublayer has nothing to read. Removing it leaves masked self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward layer per block ([[decoder-only-stack]]) — the block drawn on the left of [[fig-1]].

The cost is standing: no position ever sees its right context, in this stage or in the next one.

Masking buys causality that a recurrent network gets by construction. The paper's own measurement of that trade is the swap to a single-layer LSTM, which costs 5.6 average points ([[ablation-lstm-substitution]]).

chapters.title: Equation 2, Line by Line
chapters.body:
[[eq-decoder-stack|Equation 2]] is three lines. Take them in order.

Line one. $U$ is the context written as one-hot rows, so $UW_e$ is a matrix product on paper and a row lookup in practice: token $u$ fetches row $u$ of [[token-embedding-matrix]]. Each row is 768 numbers wide ([[hidden-state-dimension-768]]), and there is one row per entry of the subword vocabulary ([[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1]]).

Then $W_p$ is added. Added, not concatenated — [[input-representation-h0]] hands position and identity the same 768 coordinates to share, rather than reserving a slice of the vector for each.

$W_p$ is a trained table with one row per slot ([[learned-position-embeddings]]). It has as many rows as the window and none beyond; the sinusoids it replaces are defined at any index, and a table is not. The paper states the substitution without reporting a comparison.

Line two is $h_l = \text{transformer\_block}(h_{l-1})$, applied $n$ times. Shape in equals shape out, which is what makes the blocks stackable at all, and what later lets the analysis carry over some of them rather than all.

Line three is $P(u) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^{\mathsf{T}})$. Read the multiplication as inner products: the 768-dimensional state at the top is dotted against every row of the embedding table, giving one score per vocabulary entry ([[output-softmax-tied-embeddings]]).

So a token scores high exactly when the final state points along that token's own input embedding.

Two consequences follow. The output layer costs no parameters of its own, saving a matrix of vocabulary size by 768. And every row of $W_e$ takes gradient from two directions: wherever that token appeared as input, and at every position where it stood as a candidate.

chapters.title: The Numbers the Stack Was Built With
chapters.body:
[[model-specification]] pins the stack down: twelve blocks ([[twelve-layer-depth]]), 768-dimensional states, twelve attention heads in each block ([[twelve-attention-heads]]), and a feed-forward sublayer whose inner width is 3072 ([[position-wise-feedforward-3072]]).

Two of those numbers settle a third the paper never prints. Twelve heads splitting 768 dimensions leaves each head a 64-dimensional subspace to attend in.

The feed-forward width is really a ratio: 3072 is four times 768. Each block expands its representation fourfold, applies a nonlinearity, then projects back down to 768.

That nonlinearity is [[gelu]] rather than ReLU. It multiplies each input by the probability that a standard normal draw falls below it, so instead of a hard cut at zero the curve bends through it.

The size is worth working out, since no parameter count is reported. Attention in one block uses four $768 \times 768$ projections, about 2.4M weights. The feed-forward sublayer uses $768 \times 3072$ twice, about 4.7M. That is roughly 7.1M per block, so about 85M across the twelve, with a further 31M or so sitting in the embedding table.

Initialization is $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$ for every weight ([[weight-initialization]]). The paper's stated reason is that [[layer-normalization-gpt1]] is used throughout the stack, so a simple scheme sufficed. It offers no experiment behind that.

Depth is the one of these dimensions the paper later turns as a dial. [[fig-2]] varies how many of the twelve pre-trained blocks are carried into fine-tuning ([[layers-transferred]]) and reports the score climbing with each one added.

chapters.title: What Stage One Hands Over
chapters.body:
Stage one's output is a distribution over the vocabulary, and that distribution is not what gets used next. What crosses into the second stage is the fitted parameters ([[transfer-learning]]).

And it is not a partial handover. Because the output layer is the transposed embedding matrix, there is no separate head to discard — every weight the language model has is a weight the next stage inherits ([[supervised-fine-tuning]]).

The loss itself is not discarded either. $L_1$ returns during fine-tuning as a second term sitting alongside the task loss ([[auxiliary-lm-objective]]).

What the paper wants from all this is stated plainly enough. The objective never names a task, so any task-relevant ability in the weights arrives as a byproduct of predicting text ([[task-agnostic-model]]).

The conclusion claims that training this way leaves the model with knowledge about the world ([[world-knowledge]]). The analysis section puts a mechanism to it as a hypothesis: the generative model picks up abilities the evaluation tasks need because those abilities improve its language modelling, and the transformer's more structured attentional memory assists transfer compared with a recurrent state ([[transformer-inductive-bias]]).

Both are hypotheses in the paper's own wording. Nothing in the objective or the architecture establishes them; the measurements that bear on them come later.

n-the-corpus-and-the-training-run.title: The Corpus, the Model, the Run
n-the-corpus-and-the-training-run.intro: The parent listed the choices. This level shows the mechanisms behind them: what sentence-level shuffling actually removes and what the paper never tested, how raw book text becomes 40,000-merge subword units, how the dimensions of one block fit together, and what a 100-epoch run costs in updates. It ends where the parent ended, on a single perplexity number, and says what that number does and does not establish.

chapters.title: The Corpus as an Argument
chapters.body:
The case for [[bookscorpus]] is comparative, and it repays separating what the comparison establishes from what it assumes.

Both corpora are about the same size. Size is therefore held fixed, and one property differs: order. Shuffling the [[one-billion-word-benchmark|1B Word Benchmark]] at the sentence level leaves every unigram, every bigram and every within-sentence dependency exactly where it was. What it removes is any statistical relation between one sentence and the next one.

Name those relations concretely. A pronoun and the name it stands for, several sentences back, is [[coreference]]. A character introduced in one paragraph and referred to by role in the next is another. These are the [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|far-apart relations]] that [[language-modeling-objective|the objective]] can only learn if the training text contains them at all.

Now the sampling. Each training sequence is a contiguous run of 512 tokens taken from one book, not 512 tokens assembled from separate pieces. In a shuffled corpus the window would still be full. Most of what filled it would simply be unrelated to the token being predicted. The window is [[context-window-512-tokens|as wide as $k$ allows]] either way; only in [[long-range-contiguous-text|ordered text]] does the extra width carry anything.

Then the part the paper leaves open. It runs no control. It does not pre-train the same model on the shuffled corpus and compare the downstream numbers. Contiguity is given as a reason for a choice, not tested as a hypothesis — [[generative-pretraining|stage one]] was run once, on books.

One thing the choice does not claim to secure. Books are fiction-heavy; the evaluation tasks include news, science exam questions and Wikipedia. The paper's stated position is [[domain-mismatch-tolerance|that no domain match is required]].

chapters.title: Raw Text to Subword Units
chapters.body:
The [[text-preprocessing-pipeline|three steps]] each do a separate job.

[[ftfy]] goes first. Raw book text carries encoding damage: characters mangled by a bad decode, curly and straight quotes mixed together, irregular whitespace. ftfy repairs that and standardizes some punctuation and whitespace. The step matters more than it sounds, because every surface variant the cleaner fails to merge becomes its own set of subword pieces further down.

The [[spacy-tokenizer|spaCy tokenizer]] then cuts the cleaned text into word-level tokens, splitting punctuation off words and handling contractions.

Then [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1|byte-pair encoding]]. Start with each word written as its sequence of characters. Count every adjacent symbol pair across the corpus. Take the most frequent pair and record it as a merge: those two symbols are now one symbol. Recount. Merge again. Repeat.

Each merge adds exactly one symbol to the vocabulary. Frequent sequences rise to the top early, so ordinary words become single symbols within the first few thousand merges. Rare words never top the frequency list as wholes, so they stay split into pieces that other words also use.

[[bpe-merges-40000|40,000 merges]] is the entire setting, and it trades two ways. Too few, and almost everything splits toward characters: sequences get longer, and a fixed window spans less text. Too many, and the vocabulary grows while each rare embedding is trained on fewer occurrences.

Two consequences follow. There is no unknown token, since any string decomposes into pieces already present, down to single characters. And the vocabulary size fixes the shape of the largest matrix in the model: the [[token-embedding-matrix|token embedding matrix $W_e$]], which enters at [[input-representation-h0|$h_0$]] and returns transposed in the [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|output softmax]].

chapters.title: How the Dimensions Fit Together
chapters.body:
The numbers in the [[model-specification|specification]] are not four independent choices.

[[hidden-state-dimension-768|768]] divided by [[twelve-attention-heads|12 heads]] gives each head a 64-dimensional subspace to attend in. The [[position-wise-feedforward-3072|3072-dimensional]] inner layer is $4 \times 768$: each block expands fourfold and projects back down. Both ratios come straight from the original transformer.

Walk the parameter count, which the paper does not report. Inside one block, the attention sublayer holds four $768 \times 768$ projections — queries, keys, values, output — at $589{,}824$ each, so about $2.4$M. The feed-forward sublayer holds $768 \times 3072$ going up and $3072 \times 768$ coming back, about $4.7$M. That is roughly $7$M per block, and [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve blocks]] of it come to around $85$M. Add roughly $31$M for a 40,000-row embedding table of width 768. The [[decoder-only-stack|single stack]] is therefore on the order of a hundred million parameters.

Three smaller choices are stated, two with reasons and one without.

[[learned-position-embeddings|Position embeddings are learned]] rather than sinusoidal. That makes the window a parameter shape: $W_p$ has exactly 512 rows, one per slot, and nothing is defined beyond them.

[[gelu|GELU]] replaces ReLU. It computes $x\,\Phi(x)$, gating each input by the probability that a standard normal draw falls below it — smooth everywhere, and slightly negative for small negative inputs. No ablation is offered for it.

Initialization is a plain $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$ draw, and the paper says [[weight-initialization|that sufficed]] because [[layer-normalization-gpt1|layer normalization]] is used throughout the stack.

The depth is also a dial the [[layers-transferred|transfer analysis]] turns later.

chapters.title: The Run, Counted in Updates
chapters.body:
The [[pre-training-optimization|optimization setup]] is easier to judge once the schedule is counted in updates rather than epochs.

One minibatch is 64 sequences of 512 tokens, which is $32{,}768$ tokens per update. The [[linear-warmup|warmup]] runs 2000 updates, so the learning rate climbs from zero to $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ over roughly $65$M tokens. If the corpus is on the order of a billion tokens, warmup is a small fraction of the first pass alone. [[pretraining-schedule|100 passes]] over such a corpus works out to a few million updates in total.

Why warm up at all. [[adam-optimizer-gpt1|Adam]] scales each step by running estimates of the gradient's first and second moments, and those estimates are built from almost no data at the start. Full-size steps taken on them are steps taken on noise.

After the peak, [[cosine-annealing|the rate follows a cosine curve]] back to zero across the remaining updates. The curve spends a long stretch near the peak and slows late, and the endpoint is zero rather than a floor.

The [[regularization-setup|regularizers]] are three plus one. [[dropout-gpt1|Dropout]] at rate 0.1 is applied [[residual-embedding-attention-dropout|on residual branches, at the embedding layer, and inside attention]]. Alongside it runs a [[decoupled-weight-decay|modified L2 penalty]] at $w = 0.01$, applied to every weight that is not a bias or a gain. The exclusion is deliberate: layer normalization's gains and biases exist to rescale activations, and shrinking them toward zero would work against the normalization.

No compute cost, wall-clock time or sweep over these settings is reported.

chapters.title: What 18.4 Establishes
chapters.body:
[[token-level-perplexity|18.4]] is the exponential of the mean negative log-likelihood per token. Loosely, at each position the model is about as uncertain as someone choosing uniformly among eighteen options.

Two qualifications sit on the number.

The token is a BPE unit, not a word. Splitting rare words into pieces produces more tokens, and each piece is individually easier to predict than the whole rare word would have been, so a token-level figure is not comparable with a word-level one on the same text.

And the paper reports the figure on the corpus, without naming a held-out split. After 100 passes over that corpus, a number stated this way does not separate fit from generalization. It is offered as evidence that [[maximum-likelihood-training|maximizing likelihood]] did what it was asked to do.

That is the limit of what it carries. A perplexity says nothing about whether the weights help on a labelled task, which is the only thing [[two-stage-training-procedure|the recipe]] is finally judged on. The paper does not argue from it either. Its evidence that pre-training matters comes later, from [[ablation-no-pretraining|the ablation that removes pre-training]] and from [[zero-shot-behaviors|heuristics run on the generative model directly]], not from this line. The claim in the conclusion that the model has picked up [[world-knowledge|knowledge about the world]] rests on those, not on 18.4.

What the number does mark is the end of stage one. From here the same weights stop being a language model and start being an initialization for [[supervised-fine-tuning|something else]].

n-from-language-model-to-classifier.title: From Language Model to Classifier
n-from-language-model-to-classifier.intro: The summary said what stage two does: read the last token, multiply by one matrix, keep the language modelling loss running, train briefly. This level asks the questions that answer skips — why that position and not another, what the gradient actually touches, what the second loss is computed on, and what the reported settings amount to on a small dataset versus a large one.

chapters.title: Reading the Last Position
chapters.body:
Start with the choice of where to read.

The stack is causally masked: under [[masked-self-attention]] the activation at position $i$ has attended to positions $1$ through $i$ and nothing after. So the final block's output at position 1 has seen one token. The output at position $m$ has seen all $m$.

Only the last position is a summary of the whole input. That is why [[eq-task-head]] reads [[final-token-activation]] rather than pooling across positions — under this masking, no other single position has the whole sequence available.

What sits on top of it is small. The activation is a 768-dimensional vector ([[hidden-state-dimension-768]]), so [[linear-output-layer-wy]] is a $768 \times |Y|$ matrix. For a three-way inference task that is 2,304 numbers, added to a stack of twelve blocks ([[twelve-layer-depth]]), each with a 3072-dimensional inner feed-forward layer. The paper never states a total parameter count, but the ratio is not close.

Notice what the head is not. There is no hidden layer, no task-specific attention, no learned pooling. Any nonlinear work a task needs has to already be available inside the pre-trained blocks, because the only thing between them and the label scores is one matrix multiply and a softmax.

The paper does not argue for this. It writes Equation 3 and lets the scoreboard carry the claim.

[[minimal-extra-parameters]] is the tally: $W_y$, plus embeddings for the [[delimiter-token]] that separates the parts of an input. [[fig-1]] draws this head and the language modelling head sitting on the same stack. Which token sequence gets fed in is a separate question, handled in the next chapter over.

chapters.title: What the Label Loss Actually Moves
chapters.body:
[[eq-supervised-objective]] has the same shape as the pre-training loss. Both are [[maximum-likelihood-training]]: sum a log-probability the model assigns to something observed.

The difference is what is being summed over. $L_1$ runs over token positions and scores a distribution over the vocabulary. [[supervised-objective-l2]] runs over instances in [[labeled-dataset-c]] and scores a distribution over that task's labels.

Write it that way and the only thing separating one task from another is which $\mathcal{C}$ you plug in.

Now the part the equation leaves implicit. Nothing in $L_2$ restricts the gradient to $W_y$. The loss is differentiated through the whole stack, so every pre-trained weight moves — embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, all twelve blocks.

That is worth separating from the parameter-count claim. "Only $W_y$ is added" is a statement about what has to be freshly initialized. It is not a claim that the rest is frozen. Each fine-tuned task ends up owning a full, separately modified copy of the stack.

This is what distinguishes the recipe from [[feature-based-transfer]]. There the pre-trained model is held fixed and its hidden states are fed as features into a task network trained from scratch, as in [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations]]. The [[per-task-parameter-cost]] in that setup is a whole new model per task. Here it is one matrix, bought at the price of updating everything behind it.

Which raises the obvious worry. A twelve-block stack is being fitted on [[rte]]'s 2,490 training examples, or [[sts-b]]'s roughly 5,700.

The paper does not confront overfitting directly. It adds a second loss.

chapters.title: Why the Old Loss Stays On
chapters.body:
Look closely at the argument in [[eq-combined-objective]]. The auxiliary term is $L_1(\mathcal{C})$, not $L_1(U)$.

So the next-token loss is no longer computed on [[bookscorpus]]. It runs on the task's own labelled inputs, read simply as text. A premise, a delimiter and a hypothesis get scored token by token as if they were a passage from a book, at the same time as they are scored for their label.

The machinery for that is already present. The language modelling head is the transposed token embedding matrix ([[output-softmax-tied-embeddings]], reusing [[token-embedding-matrix]]), so keeping [[auxiliary-lm-objective]] switched on costs no new parameters at all. A model with a separately trained output projection would have had to carry one along on purpose.

[[auxiliary-objective-weight]] sets the balance at $0.5$. The paper reports the value in its setup section, and does not report searching over it or testing how sensitive results are to it.

The two stated benefits — better generalization, faster convergence — are given as findings, not as consequences of an argument. No mechanism is offered. Prior work is cited as having seen the same thing.

Then the paper's own ablation complicates it. Removing the term ([[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] in [[table-5]]) raises the unweighted average by 0.3 points. It helps on the inference tasks and on [[qqp]], and hurts on the smaller sets, which the paper reads as a size trend.

So the default configuration carries a term whose average measured effect, in this paper, is slightly negative.

One more thing has happened here. [[auxiliary-training-objectives]] appeared in the related work as a rival branch, the transfer mechanism in its own right. Here the same device is demoted to a supplement sitting on top of pre-training.

chapters.title: Three Passes at a Quarter of the Rate
chapters.body:
[[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] states a default: unless the paper says otherwise, stage two keeps stage one's settings. [[adam-optimizer-gpt1]] stays, [[regularization-setup]] stays, the vocabulary stays.

The exceptions are few, and each is a step down in scale.

The rate is $6.25\text{e-}5$ ([[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch]]). Divide [[pre-training-optimization]]'s peak of $2.5\text{e-}4$ by it and you get exactly 4. Batch size drops from 64 sequences to 32. Since a pre-training batch was 64 contiguous sequences of 512 tokens ([[pretraining-schedule]]), about 32,768 tokens, a fine-tuning batch is smaller in tokens too, by however short the task inputs happen to be.

The schedule changes shape as well. Pre-training annealed on a cosine curve ([[cosine-annealing]]); [[fine-tuning-lr-schedule]] decays linearly to zero.

And the warmup is now relative. Pre-training warmed up over a fixed 2,000 updates ([[linear-warmup]]); fine-tuning warms up over the first 0.2% of training.

Walk that through. [[snli]] has around 550,000 training examples, so [[three-epochs-fine-tuning]] at batch 32 is about 51,500 updates, and 0.2% of that is roughly 103 updates of warmup. [[rte]] has 2,490 examples: about 233 updates in total, and 0.2% of that is under half of one. The same rule gives a real warmup on the largest set and none at all on the smallest. The paper does not comment on this.

The only addition is [[classifier-dropout]] at 0.1 on the new head.

Read against [[ulmfit]]'s staged schedule, the point of this list is what is missing from it. No layer-wise rates, no unfreezing order. Three passes, one rate, decay to zero — and, the paper hedges, that sufficed for most datasets.

n-one-sequence-per-task.title: One Sequence Per Task
n-one-sequence-per-task.intro: The parent said where the paper puts the task's structure: in the input, not the architecture. This level says why that is the only place it can go given what sits on top of the stack, what each of the four input shapes costs to run, and what the parameter claim does and does not cover.

chapters.title: What the Other Option Actually Was
chapters.body:
Start with the alternative, drawn concretely.

The systems this paper measures itself against are mostly task-built recurrent networks ([[baseline-comparisons]]). For an entailment dataset that typically means a biLSTM reading each sentence, an attention mechanism aligning one against the other, and a classifier on the aligned result. Under [[feature-based-transfer]] — [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations]] is the named case — the transferred part is a set of contextual vectors, and that pairing network is built on top of them.

Two things follow from that arrangement.

The pairing network starts from random weights. And it learns from exactly one source: the target task's labelled examples.

So the component that does the structural work — the part that actually knows there are two sentences and has to relate them — is the component trained on the least data. That is the sharp form of the paper's objection. Counted in parameters rather than in data, the same objection is the [[per-task-parameter-cost]] complaint, and the scarcity it runs into is the one the paper opened on ([[labeled-data-scarcity]]).

The paper's replacement is credited to earlier work, not claimed as its own: it cites the [[traversal-style-approach]] and applies it.

But the swap has a price, and the paper does not dwell on it. [[structured-inputs]] arrive with their parts already separated and named. After the transformation, the only surviving trace of that structure is token order plus one symbol. Whatever the pairing network was computing explicitly, the stack must now compute implicitly, using weights trained only to predict the next word. The paper does not argue that this suffices. It reports scores for [[task-agnostic-model]] instead, and lets them carry the point.

chapters.title: One Vector, at One Position
chapters.body:
The transformations look like a stylistic choice until you look at what consumes their output.

[[eq-task-head]] is the whole task-specific classifier. Take the final block's activation at the last input token ([[final-token-activation]]), multiply by one matrix ([[linear-output-layer-wy]]), softmax.

Notice what the head never receives. It does not read the sequence. It reads a single vector, at a single position.

And because attention is masked ([[masked-self-attention]]), that position is the only one that could serve. Every earlier token was forbidden from attending rightward, so only the last position has seen the whole input.

The format therefore has one hard requirement: that last position must exist and must mean the same thing in every example. This is the job of [[start-and-end-tokens]]. Each transformed input is wrapped, so the vector the classifier reads is always the activation over $\langle e\rangle$ — never over whatever content word happened to land last, which would vary example to example.

The [[delimiter-token]] handles the complementary job inside the sequence, marking where one part stops and the next starts.

Both symbols are new. Neither occurred during pre-training, so their embeddings are initialized randomly and fitted during fine-tuning alone — three passes over the task's labelled set, at a learning rate of $6.25\times10^{-5}$ ([[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]]).

That is a thin budget for symbols that have to come to mean "a boundary happens here" and "the input ends here". The paper reports the recipe works; it never isolates this piece. No ablation removes the brackets or the delimiter, so how much of the result rests on them is untested.

One small ambiguity: the delimiter is written `$`, a character books already contain, yet delimiter embeddings are counted among the parameters a new task adds. So it is being treated as its own entry in the [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1]] vocabulary, not as the ordinary currency symbol reused.

chapters.title: Four Shapes, and What Each Costs to Run
chapters.body:
The four templates are not equally cheap, and the differences are worth naming.

[[text-classification]] needs no transformation at all. A single sentence already is one ordered run of tokens, so those datasets are fine-tuned directly.

Entailment adds one symbol and nothing else: premise, delimiter, hypothesis, one forward pass ([[entailment-input-transformation]]). The task hands over the order, so there is no decision to make.

Similarity is where the readout bites. The stack runs left to right and summarizes at the end, so whichever sentence is placed second sits nearer the summary, while the first has to survive the whole second sentence to reach it. Picking an order would make the prediction depend on an arbitrary choice the task never made.

So both orderings are built, each is run through the stack on its own, and the two final activations are added before the linear layer ([[similarity-input-transformation]]). Element-wise addition is symmetric, so swapping which sentence you called first leaves the head's input unchanged. The fix costs two forward passes per example.
