Question answering has a different problem: the number of candidates varies, and a fixed architecture cannot have a variable number of output slots. Building $[z; q; \$; a_k]$ once per candidate sidesteps that by running the same fixed model several times ([[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]]). The softmax then normalizes across sequences rather than across label columns inside one sequence. The paper does not state the head's shape here, but for a distribution over candidates to come out, each pass must yield a single score.

Cost scales with the option count: two passes for the two endings of the [[story-cloze-test]], more for a multi-option exam question ([[race-dataset]]).

One limit goes unmentioned. The stack reads at most 512 tokens ([[context-window-512-tokens]]), while a comprehension sequence carries a full passage plus a question plus an answer. The paper says nothing about what happens when that overflows.

[[fig-1]] draws all four beside the [[decoder-only-stack]] they feed.

chapters.title: Counting What a New Task Adds
chapters.body:
The parameter claim ([[minimal-extra-parameters]]) is checkable, so check it.

$W_y$ maps one 768-dimensional activation ([[hidden-state-dimension-768]]) to label scores. Three-way inference needs $768 \times 3$, which is $2{,}304$ weights. Binary sentiment needs $1{,}536$. Multiple choice, producing one score per sequence, needs $768$. A delimiter embedding is another $768$ numbers.

Now the denominator. From [[model-specification]], each block's self-attention holds four $768 \times 768$ matrices; $768 \times 768$ is $589{,}824$, so that sublayer is about $2.4$ million weights. The feed-forward sublayer holds two matrices of $768 \times 3072$, which is $2{,}359{,}296$ each, so about $4.7$ million more. Call it $7$ million per block. With [[twelve-layer-depth]], the stack alone is roughly $85$ million, before the token embedding table is counted.

The arithmetic is mine from the stated dimensions; the paper reports no total.

So the comparison is a couple of thousand new numbers against tens of millions of transferred ones. The claim survives.

But read what it counts. These are the parameters that start from random initialization — not the parameters that change. The supervised loss ([[eq-supervised-objective]]) backpropagates through every block, so fine-tuning moves the entire stack.

That means each of the twelve datasets ends with its own complete copy of the weights. Nothing here is shared at deployment time.

The claim is about how much untrained machinery a task requires, not about storage. Which is the right claim for the argument it answers, since the objection to the alternative was precisely that its new components learn from scratch on scarce labels.

chapters.title: Four Templates, Twelve Datasets
chapters.body:
Line the templates up against the evaluation menu ([[evaluation-task-families]], [[table-1]]) and the ratio is the point.

[[natural-language-inference]] supplies five datasets, all of them the premise-delimiter-hypothesis shape. [[semantic-similarity]] supplies three, all on the two-pass symmetric shape. [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning]] supplies two, both on the one-sequence-per-candidate shape. Classification supplies two, on no shape at all.

Five plus three plus two plus two is twelve.

So breadth of tasks is not breadth of formats. Twelve datasets are covered by four templates, one of which is the empty template. Several of the datasets come bundled in [[glue-benchmark]], which is part of why the menu could be assembled this quickly.

The sizes are not uniform either. They run from roughly $5{,}700$ training examples on [[sts-b]] up to roughly $550{,}000$ on [[snli]], a spread of about two orders of magnitude, and the paper uses that spread to argue the recipe is not only a large-data technique.

One thing the menu holds constant is worth naming, because the transformations depend on it. Every one of the twelve ends in a label from a fixed set, or a choice among candidates the dataset supplies. None asks for generated text.

That is what lets the whole task-side apparatus be a serializer plus one scoring matrix. A task whose output is itself structured would need something else, and the paper does not claim it.

[[etheme-one-stack-any-input-shape|One stack, any input shape]] — with the shapes counted, and the outputs kept simple.

n-the-scoreboard.title: Reading the Scoreboard
n-the-scoreboard.intro: The parent gave the margins. This level gives the numbers on both sides of them, the units each column is measured in, and the three rows where the model does not come first.

chapters.title: What a Point Means, and Who Is on the Other Side
chapters.body:
Before any margin means anything, two things about the tables need saying.

The first is that a "point" is not one currency. [[absolute-improvement|Gains in percentage points]] are quoted across every task, but the columns of [[table-4]] are not all measuring the same quantity. Its header spells this out: [[cola|CoLA]] is scored by Matthews correlation, [[sst-2|SST-2]] by accuracy, [[mrpc|MRPC]] and [[qqp|QQP]] by F1, [[sts-b|STS-B]] by Pearson correlation.

Matthews correlation is computed from the confusion matrix of a binary classifier and runs from $-1$ to $+1$, with $0$ at chance, reported here multiplied by 100. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall on the positive class. Pearson correlation compares the model's graded similarity scores against the human ones.

So a 10.4 move on CoLA and a 4.2 move on QQP are moves along different scales. Adding them together is exactly what an aggregate score does, and the tables do it.

The second is what the numbers are being beaten. The [[baseline-comparisons|previous bests]] are not one system but a shelf of them, each built for its own dataset, and mostly recurrent — a [[lstm-gpt1|biLSTM]] core with attention, ELMo features, or both.

Several are ensembles. [[table-2|Table 2]] annotates rows with `5x` and `3x` to mark ensembles of five and three models, and marks the previous best in each column by underlining it.

The paper's own entry is one row in each table, and it is a single model everywhere. That is the comparison being set up: one set of fine-tuned weights against a per-dataset field, some of which is voting.

chapters.title: The Numbers Behind the Margins
chapters.body:
With the units fixed, the head-to-head figures are worth reading directly.

On [[natural-language-inference|inference]], [[multinli|MultiNLI]] is reported in two columns, matched and mismatched: 82.1 and 81.4, against 80.6 and 80.1 from a three-model ensemble. The 1.5 the paper quotes is the matched column; the mismatched gain is 1.3.

[[snli|SNLI]] moves from 89.3 to 89.9. The 89.3 was posted by two separate five-model ensembles, so the 0.6 is small but taken off a crowded ceiling.

[[scitail|SciTail]] goes 83.3 to 88.3 and [[qnli|QNLI]] 82.3 to 88.1 — five and 5.8 points, both against single systems rather than ensembles.

The [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning|reading and reasoning]] numbers in [[table-3]] have more inside them than the headline. [[race-dataset|RACE]] is split into middle-school and high-school questions. Middle school goes 60.2 to 62.9, a gain of 2.7. High school goes 50.3 to 57.4, a gain of 7.1.

The 5.7 overall is a blend of those two, and it is the harder split that carries it. The system passed on both is a nine-model ensemble.

Note also the absolute level: 59.0 overall on RACE. The margin is wide, but it sits low on the scale, on a dataset picked because it holds more reasoning-type questions than the [[cnn-and-squad-contrast|extraction-style alternatives]].

[[story-cloze-test|Story Cloze]] is the widest gap on any single number, 77.6 to 86.5. The paper reads the pair as evidence about long-range context, which is an interpretation laid over the numbers, not something the numbers separate out on their own.

chapters.title: The Three Rows It Does Not Win
chapters.body:
Nine of twelve leaves three, and the tables name them.

[[rte|RTE]] is the one the paper discusses: 56.0 against 61.7 from a multi-task biLSTM. Its explanation is dataset size, 2,490 training examples, and its proposed fix is multi-task training, which it states it did not run.

The other two are quieter. On [[mrpc]] the model scores 82.3 F1 against a previous best of 86.0 — and the multi-task biLSTM in the same table scores 83.5, so this is third place, not second. On SST-2 the same pattern: 91.3 against 93.2 from the best system, with the multi-task biLSTM at 91.6 in between.

So one loss falls in [[semantic-similarity|similarity]] and one in [[text-classification|classification]], and neither is explained.

The size story does not hold on its own either. STS-B has roughly 5,700 training examples, more than twice RTE's but still the smallest set in the [[evaluation-task-families|evaluation]], and it is a win. Size alone does not sort the wins from the losses.

There is one more thing visible in the same table that the paper does not take up. The multi-task biLSTM that beats it on RTE scores 18.9 on CoLA, where the single-task version of the same architecture scores 35.0.

Multi-task training, in the paper's own comparison set, helps on some columns and costs heavily on others. That makes the suggested fix for RTE less obviously free than the sentence proposing it implies, and it remains untested here either way — one of the softer spots in the [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12|nine of twelve]] claim.

chapters.title: The Aggregate, and Where the Count Comes From
chapters.body:
Two summary numbers close the evaluation, and both are assembled rather than measured.

The [[glue-benchmark|GLUE]] score of 72.8 against 68.9 is an aggregate over the tasks in its column, so a large move anywhere inside it lifts the total. The single-task biLSTM with ELMo and attention scores 64.8 on the same aggregate; the multi-task version, 68.9.

The column that moves furthest inside that aggregate is CoLA, and CoLA is also the column whose metric is least like an accuracy. The paper reads its 45.4 as evidence of linguistic bias picked up in pre-training. That reading is plausible and the number does not settle it.

The headline count is assembled the same way. Nine of twelve appears in no table. You get it by reading three of them and counting the bold rows: four inference wins, two reading wins, [[qqp]], STS-B and CoLA — with [[table-1]] fixing the denominator at twelve datasets across four families.

What the whole board does establish is narrow and real. One pre-trained stack, fine-tuned per task with a task-shaped input and a linear head as in [[fig-1]], beats per-task systems on most rows and several ensembles among them.

What it does not establish is which part of the recipe earned that. The scoreboard measures the finished pipeline end to end, and separating the pre-training, the architecture and the auxiliary objective takes a different experiment.

[[theme-what-the-twelve-datasets-show|The twelve datasets in full]]; [[etheme-the-scoreboard-and-its-gaps|the gaps in the board]].

n-which-parts-do-the-work.title: Which Parts Do the Work, and What Is Left Open
n-which-parts-do-the-work.intro: The parent named the three diagnostics. This level reads them as experiments: what was actually varied and what was held fixed, how each panel of Figure 2 is drawn and what its axes hide, which datasets the ablation table covers, and where the paper's own numbers disagree with each other.

chapters.title: Thirteen Runs Up the Stack
chapters.body:
The left panel of [[fig-2]] is not one training run. It is a series of them, one per point.

The x-axis counts layers transferred, from 0 to 13. That is one slot for the embedding layer plus one for each block in the [[twelve-layer-depth]] stack. At position 1 only the [[token-embedding-matrix]] and the [[learned-position-embeddings]] carry over from [[generative-pretraining]]; every transformer block is initialized fresh. At 13 the whole pre-trained network carries over. Each position gets its own [[supervised-fine-tuning]] run.

So the leftmost useful point is roughly the older practice of [[word-embedding-transfer]], and the sweep asks what the blocks add on top of it.

Two datasets are plotted, and the axes are not shared. [[race-dataset]] dev accuracy reads off a left axis spanning 30 to 100, rising from about 39.7 to about 60. [[multinli]] dev accuracy reads off a right axis spanning 70 to 100, rising from about 72.5 to about 82.

That second window is a third as tall over the same plot height. A MultiNLI point therefore looks about two and a half times steeper than a RACE point of the same size. Read the colour before the slope.

Dashed lines are training accuracy from the same runs. They sit above the dev lines and climb further, so extra transferred layers also fit the labelled data harder.

What the panel licenses is the monotone total. What it does not measure is any individual layer: the sweep only ever adds blocks from the bottom up, so it never asks what layers 6 through 12 are worth on their own. The reading in [[layers-transferred]] is consistent with the curve rather than demonstrated by it, on two datasets, on dev sets, one run each.

chapters.title: Turning a Next-Token Model Into a Scorer
chapters.body:
The pre-trained model emits one thing: a distribution over the next token, formed by [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings]]. Nothing in it names a class.

To compare two candidate answers you can score each string by the summed log-probability of its tokens. That comparison is broken by length. Every token contributes a negative number, so the shorter candidate wins by default.

Divide by the token count and the bias goes away. That mean is [[average-token-log-probability-scoring]], and three of the four constructions in [[zero-shot-behaviors]] rest on it.

On RACE the model is conditioned on the document and the question, each candidate answer is scored, and the highest wins ([[race-zero-shot-heuristic]]). This is the fine-tuning-time [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]] with the classifier removed.

DPRD is a set of Winograd schemas: a definite pronoun with two possible antecedents ([[coreference]]). The heuristic substitutes each antecedent for the pronoun and scores the rest of the sequence after the substitution ([[dprd-winograd-heuristic]]). Both readings score the same trailing tokens, so length is matched exactly and only the conditioning context differs.

[[cola-zero-shot-heuristic]] is the odd one of the three. Acceptability is a single-sentence judgement with no competing candidate, so the score is compared against a threshold instead. The paper does not say how that threshold is set, which makes it a free parameter fitted somewhere outside the described procedure, unlike the three argmax constructions.

Sentiment uses a different device entirely ([[sst2-zero-shot-heuristic]]). Appending *very* and reading off the relative probability of *positive* against *negative* consults one next-token distribution, not a whole-string score. It also assumes the corpus phrases sentiment that way. The paper calls all four heuristic solutions and does not argue they are the best available ones for [[cola]] or [[sst-2]].

chapters.title: Watching the Heuristics Climb
chapters.body:
The right panel of [[fig-2]] shares nothing with the left one but the page. Its x-axis is pre-training updates on a log scale, $10^3$ to $10^6$, which is the run described in [[pre-training-optimization]] sampled as it went.

The y-axis is rescaled per task. Zero is a random-guess baseline and one is the best published single-model result on that task. A value of 0.68 means the heuristic closed 68% of that gap.

That rescaling is what lets four differently-scored tasks share an axis. It also means the ceiling is a moving reference from the [[baseline-comparisons]] of the day, and that no absolute accuracy can be read off the plot at all.

All four solid curves rise and largely stay risen. Nothing in the run is optimizing them: the only loss being minimized is [[language-modeling-objective]], and the corpus is books. The behaviours arrive as a side effect of fitting it, which the [[token-level-perplexity]] of 18.4 says was fitted well.

One alternative the panel does not separate: these heuristics all read fluency, and fluency improves with perplexity. A curve that rises with better next-token prediction is what you would see either way.

The dashed lines are an LSTM language model trained the same way. They reach lower and move around more, and the sentiment curve drops from 0.42 to 0.30 before recovering.

The paper offers this as support for [[transformer-inductive-bias]] — that attention over a wide context, restricted by [[masked-self-attention]], is a more structured memory for [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]] than a recurrent state. It is one [[lstm-gpt1]] configuration against one transformer, single runs, with variance judged by eye off a plot. The paper writes *suggesting*, and that is the right strength for it.

chapters.title: Three Removals, Eight Datasets
chapters.body:
[[table-5]] is four recipes down the side and eight datasets across the top. Those eight are the [[glue-benchmark]] tasks.

RACE and the [[story-cloze-test]] are not among them. The two datasets carrying the paper's largest margins are therefore absent from every row of its [[ablation-studies]].

The last column averages the eight numbers, unweighted. Those numbers are Matthews correlation, accuracy, F1 and Pearson correlation, so the average adds a correlation point to an accuracy point as if they were the same unit.

The full system scores 74.7. Removing pre-training gives 59.9, and $74.7 - 59.9 = 14.8$, with every column down ([[ablation-no-pretraining]]). One column dominates: CoLA falls from 45.4 to 18.9, and that 26.5-point drop divided across eight datasets contributes 3.3 of the 14.8 on its own.

The architecture swap gives 69.1, so $74.7 - 69.1 = 5.6$ ([[ablation-lstm-substitution]]). The substituted model is a single-layer LSTM of 2048 units, against twelve blocks of [[hidden-state-dimension-768]]. Depth, width and architecture all change together, so the 5.6 is not attributable to recurrence alone. The LSTM takes one column, [[mrpc]], at 83.2 against 82.3.

The third row is the one that does not behave. Fine-tuning with the supervised loss alone scores 75.0, three tenths above the full model, and takes the best cell in five of the eight columns ([[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]]).

[[auxiliary-lm-objective]] earns its keep on exactly three: [[qqp]], [[multinli|MNLI]] and QNLI. Those are the larger sets, which is the trend the paper states and the most it claims.

The recipe keeps a component that its own table scores slightly against on average, with [[auxiliary-objective-weight]] fixed at 0.5 and never swept.

chapters.title: The Numbers That Do Not Line Up
chapters.body:
[[rte]] is the clearest loss. The model reaches 56.0 against 61.7 from a multi-task biLSTM in [[table-2]], 5.7 points short, on 2,490 training examples. The paper suggests multi-task training would help and reports no such run. RTE is also one of the eight ablation columns, so the smallest set in the evaluation carries an eighth of every average in Table 5.

The GLUE figure moves between sections. [[table-4]]'s last column reads 68.9 to 72.8, and $72.8 - 68.9 = 3.9$. The introduction's headline for the same benchmark is 5.5. The paper does not reconcile the two, and the GLUE column folds in inference datasets that Table 4 does not show.

Several wins are small enough that the missing variance matters. SNLI gains 0.6 in Table 2. [[sts-b]] gains 1 point in Table 4. Every number on both sides is a single reported run against a single published best, with no repeats and no spread given.

[[state-of-the-art-9-of-12]] counts wins across [[evaluation-task-families]] without weighting them, so a 0.6 and the 8.9 in [[table-3]] each contribute one. The three that are not wins are RTE, SST-2 and [[mrpc]]. The gains are stated as [[absolute-improvement]] throughout, which keeps the arithmetic checkable.

The conclusion adds a claim the experiments do not carry. It says the model acquires significant [[world-knowledge]] from predicting long stretches of text. Every task in the evaluation rewards reading the passage in front of the model, and nothing in the design separates knowledge brought to a passage from comprehension of it.

n-the-mismatch--two-questions.title: What the Two Open Questions Were Made Of
n-the-mismatch--two-questions.intro: The parent named the two obstacles and the machinery each involved. This level opens them up: what each candidate objective actually optimizes, what kind of evidence "each outperforms the others on different tasks" is, what each transfer mechanism costs in parameters or tuning, and why the two questions were hard to separate from each other.

chapters.title: What Each Objective Actually Optimizes
chapters.body:
The first question ([[choice-of-pretraining-objective]]) gets one sentence and three citations. It does not say what any of the three optimizes. Here is what each one asks a model to produce.

Next-token prediction is the [[language-modeling-objective]]. Take a run of text, and at every position ask the model for a distribution over the vocabulary. The loss is the log-probability it assigns to the token that actually came next, summed over positions — [[maximum-likelihood-training]] and nothing more. Any text at all is training data for it.

Translation asks for a whole sentence in a second language given a sentence in the first. The part that gets reused afterwards is the encoder's hidden states, since the decoder half has no job outside translation.

The paper does not point this out, but that objective needs sentence-aligned pairs, and those pairs are annotated data. So the three candidates do not sit on the same side of [[labeled-data-scarcity]]. Two run on raw text; one runs on a parallel corpus somebody built.

Discourse coherence asks whether a group of sentences belongs together in the order given. The supervision typically comes free from the document: sentences in their original order are positives, shuffled or substituted ones are negatives. Its usual output is one vector per sentence, which places it near [[phrase-and-sentence-embeddings]].

That difference in output matters more than the introduction's single sentence suggests. [[word-embedding-transfer]] hands the next model a lookup table. A sentence encoder hands it a vector. A language model hands over every weight in the network — which is what makes [[unsupervised-pretraining]] a choice of starting point rather than a choice of features, and what keeps all of this inside [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]].

chapters.title: A Scatter, and What Would Resolve It
chapters.body:
Read the claim exactly: each *method* outperforms the others on different tasks. Not each objective. That distinction carries the whole difficulty.

A method is an objective, plus an architecture, plus a corpus, plus a way of moving the result into the target task, plus a choice of which datasets to report. Three groups built three such bundles. When one wins on sentiment and another wins on entailment, the objective is one of five things that differ.

Nothing in that comparison isolates it. And the paper does not fix the problem: it never trains a translation-objective or coherence-objective model of its own, so it never runs the head-to-head the sentence describes as unresolved.

What it runs instead is a comparison against none. [[ablation-no-pretraining]] in [[table-5]] trains the same transformer directly on the supervised tasks and loses 14.8 points on average. [[layers-transferred]] in [[fig-2]] carries a growing number of pre-trained layers into fine-tuning and finds each one adds. A [[token-level-perplexity]] of 18.4 says the objective was fit well, and [[zero-shot-behaviors]] says the fitted model already performs some of the tasks.

Every one of those measures pre-training against no pre-training. None measures language modelling against translation. The choice is defended as useful, not as best, which is a weaker claim than the question asked for.

The footnote is the honest part. It points at the [[glue-benchmark]] leaderboard rather than at a paper. A leaderboard is a number that changes, so citing one as evidence about which objective transfers says the ordering was still moving. That board scores the same [[natural-language-understanding]] tasks the paper later reports on ([[evaluation-task-families]], [[baseline-comparisons]]).

chapters.title: Three Kinds of Machinery, Three Kinds of Cost
chapters.body:
[[how-to-transfer-representations]] gets a list of three, each with its own citation. Resolve the citations and the three become concrete.

Task-specific architecture changes first. The transferred representation goes in at the bottom, and above it sits a network shaped around one task: an attention layer between premise and hypothesis for entailment, a pooling scheme for classification, and so on. [[task-specific-architectures]] means these get designed, tuned and trained from scratch, once per task. Neither the design work nor the weights carry to the next task.

Intricate learning schemes second. The citation the introduction attaches here is the same work the related-work section describes as fine-tuning a pre-trained LSTM language model on a staged schedule ([[ulmfit]], inside [[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]] alongside [[semi-supervised-sequence-learning]]).

The cost there is not parameters. It is schedule: which layers unfreeze in which epoch, a separate learning rate per layer, a shaped rate curve. Those numbers have to be found per task.

Extra unsupervised loss terms third. [[auxiliary-training-objectives]] adds a second loss to the supervised one and optimizes the sum, so raw text keeps shaping the weights while the labels do. The cost is one weight to tune and the compute of a second head.

Now the honest part. The paper does not drop the third mechanism — it keeps it. Fine-tuning here optimizes [[auxiliary-lm-objective]], with [[auxiliary-objective-weight]] set to 0.5, and the paper's own [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] reports the benefit is uneven: larger datasets gain from the term, smaller ones do not.

So the complaint is not that these mechanisms fail. It is that three were in use at once, each traced to a different paper, and nobody had removed them one at a time. The ablation table later in this paper is what doing so looks like.

chapters.title: Frozen Features, and the Metric the Paper Picks
chapters.body:
A fourth option sits slightly apart from those three, and the paper puts it in the related-work section rather than the introduction.

[[feature-based-transfer]]: freeze the pre-trained model, run the input through it, take the hidden states out, and hand them to a separate task model as extra input vectors alongside that model's own embeddings. The best-known instance is [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations]], where the states come from a pre-trained bidirectional language model.

Note what does not happen. No gradient from the task loss reaches the pre-trained weights. They are a fixed function from tokens to vectors, and everything that learns the task is new.

That is where [[per-task-parameter-cost]] comes from. The paper's phrase is that such approaches involve a substantial amount of new parameters for each separate target task. It is choosing a metric: count the freshly initialized parameters a new task requires. On that metric its own side reads [[minimal-extra-parameters]] — one [[linear-output-layer-wy]], plus embeddings for the [[delimiter-token]]s that [[task-specific-input-transformations]] introduces through its [[traversal-style-approach]].

The metric is not neutral. A frozen model has advantages the count does not see. Its states can be computed once and cached across every epoch. No gradients flow through the deep stack. One copy of the pre-trained weights serves all tasks at the same time.

Fine-tuning gives up all three. It needs a full backward pass through every layer, and it ends with a separate copy of the entire model per task.

The paper does not weigh those costs against each other. It picks the parameter count, on which its own approach wins, and moves on.

chapters.title: Why the Two Questions Compound
chapters.body:
The paragraph ends with a diagnosis: these two uncertainties are why effective semi-supervised approaches for language had been hard to build. The question is why two open problems should compound rather than simply add.

They compound because the objective constrains the transfer. A translation model's usable half is an encoder, so its output arrives as features and a task network has to be built to consume them. A sentence encoder hands over one vector per sentence, and anything the task needs below that level must come from elsewhere.

A language model is the case where the whole stack comes across. That is the one setting in which [[transfer-learning]] can mean keeping every weight and continuing to train it.

The citations show the tangle directly. The work cited for the language modelling objective is also cited for task-specific architecture changes. The work cited for translation is also cited as a source of auxiliary features. Nobody was varying one factor at a time, because each published system was a single point rather than a row in a grid.

That shape explains what the rest of the paper does. It fixes one objective and one transfer style — [[generative-pretraining]] followed by fine-tuning, together the [[two-stage-training-procedure]] — and then holds the architecture constant across every task, which is what [[task-agnostic-model]] means here.

Its argument against recurrent predecessors ([[lstm-short-range-limitation]]) and its count of [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12]] are both attempts to make one point in that grid carry the case. Neither closes the comparison the introduction says is open. They argue that this pairing works, not that it is the right one.

n-which-family-this-joins--closest-line.title: Nearly the Same Recipe
n-which-family-this-joins--closest-line.intro: The parent gave you the shape of the argument: same recipe, two claimed differences, one of them barely measured. This level opens each piece up — what the two earlier systems actually trained, what the short-range sentence is asserting step by step, and how much weight each experiment can carry once you look at what it varied.

chapters.title: What the Two Predecessors Actually Trained
chapters.body:
[[semi-supervised-sequence-learning]] is the earlier of the two works named under [[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]], and its pre-training stage came in two forms.

One was the [[language-modeling-objective]]: read unlabelled text and predict the next token. The other was a sequence autoencoder: read a sequence into a recurrent state, then train the network to emit that same sequence back out. Either way the pre-trained weights were those of an [[lstm-gpt1]], and either way the second stage was [[supervised-fine-tuning|supervised fine-tuning]] of the whole network for [[text-classification]].

[[ulmfit]] kept only the language modelling half. It pre-trained an LSTM language model, then fine-tuned it for classification on a schedule that was staged rather than uniform — different layers brought in at different points, with the learning rate shaped to match.

That staging is worth holding onto, because this paper cites the same work twice for two different reasons.

In the related work section it appears as the closest line. In the introduction it appears in the list of things that make [[how-to-transfer-representations]] an open question, under the heading of intricate learning schemes.

So the paper is not only claiming a different architecture. It is also claiming that its own second stage is plainer than ULMFiT's: [[three-epochs-fine-tuning]] for most datasets, and [[minimal-extra-parameters]] on top of the pre-trained stack.

That difference is never argued in the related work section. It is stated as a property of [[two-stage-training-procedure]] elsewhere, and left there. Only [[unsupervised-pretraining]] as a category, and the range claim, are put forward here as the separation.

chapters.title: One Sentence, and the Chain Inside It
chapters.body:
[[lstm-short-range-limitation]] is a single clause: the predecessors' use of LSTMs restricts their prediction ability to a short range. Unpacked, it is two steps, and only the second is about transfer.

The first step is about what a recurrent network can learn at all. Everything it knows about the prefix lives in one fixed-size state, rewritten at every token. A dependency reaching back four hundred tokens has to survive four hundred overwrites of that state to affect the prediction.

The second step is the transfer consequence. If pre-training never taught the model to condition on such a dependency, the pre-trained weights hold nothing about it to carry into the target task. Whatever linguistic information the phase does capture, the reach of the transferred model is capped by the reach of the pre-trained one.

The paper's alternative is stated as a property of [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]]. [[masked-self-attention]] lets every position take a direct weighted read of every earlier position, with no compression through time in between, and [[context-window-512-tokens]] fixes how far back that reach extends.

The corpus is chosen so the window has something to reach across. [[bookscorpus]] supplies [[long-range-contiguous-text]] — sentences and paragraphs in their original order — where the [[one-billion-word-benchmark]] used by [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations]] is shuffled at the sentence level.

What is never supplied is a number. The paper does not say what range an LSTM reaches, nor what range its own model reaches, nor how [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]] such as [[coreference]] across sentences fare under either. The sentence ends with a forward pointer to the experiments.

chapters.title: The One Controlled Swap, and What It Varied
chapters.body:
Of the three rows in [[ablation-studies]], reported in [[table-5]], one speaks to the range claim. [[ablation-lstm-substitution]] holds the framework fixed — same input transformations, same fine-tuning procedure, same objective — and replaces the transformer with a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM. The average score falls by 5.6 points.

Read that configuration against [[model-specification]]. The transformer is [[twelve-layer-depth]] with [[hidden-state-dimension-768]] states. The LSTM is one layer, of 2048 units.

So the swap changes two things at once: recurrence for attention, and depth twelve for depth one. The paper's own layer analysis says depth carries value, which means part of the 5.6 may be depth rather than range.

The exception is [[mrpc]], the [[semantic-similarity]] dataset built from news sentence pairs, and the only dataset where the LSTM comes out ahead. The paper reports the exception in one clause and does not account for it. The pairs there are short, which is where a limit on reach should cost least — but the paper does not say that, and neither does the table.

For scale, the same table reports [[ablation-no-pretraining]] at 14.8 points. Architecture is worth roughly a third of what stage one is worth, on the paper's own averaging, while [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] moves the average by far less than either.

All of which leaves 5.6 as a scalar summarising a set of dataset scores. Nothing in it is indexed by distance, so nothing in it separates a range effect from any other advantage the transformer might have.

chapters.title: Two Diagnostics That Point Sideways
chapters.body:
[[layers-transferred]] is the left panel of [[fig-2]]. Dev accuracy on [[multinli]] and [[race-dataset]] is plotted against how many pre-trained blocks are carried into fine-tuning. Transferring the embeddings alone already helps, and each further block adds more, reaching up to 9% for full transfer on MultiNLI.

The conclusion drawn is that every layer holds function worth carrying. That is a claim about how much of the stack transfers.

It is not a claim about how far back a prediction reaches. A curve rising with depth would look the same whether the extra layers bought range, abstraction, or capacity.

The right panel tracks [[zero-shot-behaviors]]: four heuristics, three of them built on [[average-token-log-probability-scoring]], run against the generative model across pre-training checkpoints with no fine-tuning at all. The scores rise steadily and stay stable.

[[transformer-inductive-bias]] is the hypothesis attached to that panel — that attention gives a more structured memory than a recurrent state, and that this is what assists transfer. The evidence offered for it is one observation: the LSTM shows higher variance in its zero-shot scores.

Higher variance across checkpoints is instability. It is not reach.

The paper's own verb is suggesting, twice in that paragraph, and the hedge is fair. Put together, the range claim rests on an averaged score gap, a depth curve, a variance observation, and a design argument about a 512-token window over contiguous book text. Each is consistent with the claim. None of them measures it.

chapters.title: The Difference You Can Check by Inspection
chapters.body:
The second claimed difference asks nothing of the reader beyond looking at [[table-1]]. [[evaluation-task-families]] covers four families and twelve datasets, where the predecessors reported [[text-classification]].

Walk the list. Five datasets are [[natural-language-inference]], from [[snli]] at roughly 550k training examples down to [[rte]] at 2490. Two are [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning]], including the [[story-cloze-test]], where a multi-sentence story has to be finished with the right one of two endings. Three are [[semantic-similarity]], among them [[qqp]] and [[sts-b]] at about 5.7k examples. Two are single-sentence classification, one of which is [[sst-2]].

So ten of the twelve sit outside the task type the earlier work reported on. Only the last two are the same kind of problem.

That is a fact about which datasets were run, not an inference from a score gap. It survives whatever you conclude about range.

And it is carried by a different part of the paper. Breadth comes from [[task-agnostic-model]] plus the input transformations that fold ordered pairs and document-question-answer triples into one token sequence. Nothing in that argument depends on choosing attention over recurrence.

The headline that follows — [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12]] — is likewise a count, not a mechanism.

Which leaves the two claimed differences resting on very different footings. One is asserted, pointed forward, and then supported indirectly. The other is simply exhibited.

n-predicting-the-next-token--stack-dimen.title: The Numbers the Stack Was Built With
n-predicting-the-next-token--stack-dimen.intro: The parent listed the dimensions. This level takes them one at a time and asks what each one actually controls inside a block, what it costs in weights or activations, and what the paper offers as a reason for it — which, for most of them, is nothing.

chapters.title: The Width That Nothing Is Allowed to Change
chapters.body:
Of the numbers in [[model-specification]], 768 is the least free. It is not a per-layer setting that happens to be held constant. Three separate places in [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]] pin it to the same value at once.

The first is the input. [[input-representation-h0]] adds token embeddings and position embeddings together, so both tables must produce vectors of the same width, and that width becomes the width of everything downstream.

The second is the residual stream. Each block adds its sublayer outputs back into the state it received, so whatever a block computes internally, it must hand back something of the same shape it was given.

The third is the output. [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings]] scores the vocabulary by multiplying the top state by the transpose of the embedding table. That product only makes sense if a top-layer state is the same length as one row of [[token-embedding-matrix]].

So [[hidden-state-dimension-768]] is one decision made once, not twelve.

It is also where a large block of weights sits outside the stack. [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1]] with [[bpe-merges-40000]] gives a vocabulary of roughly forty thousand entries. Forty thousand rows of 768 numbers is 30.7M weights. [[learned-position-embeddings]] add one row per slot in the [[context-window-512-tokens]], so 512 by 768, about 0.4M more.

Tying means that table is read twice per forward pass — once to look up, once transposed to score — and receives gradient from both.

chapters.title: Twelve Heads, and What They Do Not Cost
chapters.body:
Head count is the one dimension here that is free in parameters.

A block's attention uses four square projections — query, key, value, and the output projection that recombines. Each is 768 by 768, whatever the head count. [[twelve-attention-heads]] does not add a thirteenth matrix; it slices the three input projections into twelve strips of 768 by 64 and lets each strip run its own attention. The recombining matrix then stitches the twelve 64-dimensional results back into 768. Four times 589,824 is about 2.4M weights, and that figure is the same for one head or for twelve.

What the count does change is how many distinct attention patterns a block can hold. One head must fold all its evidence about the past into a single softmax over positions. Twelve can keep twelve, which matters for the [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]] the paper is after, where one head might track the nearest few tokens while another reaches back hundreds.

The 64-dimensional subspace also sets the scale inside the softmax: dot products are divided by $\sqrt{64}$, which is 8.

The real cost is activations. Under [[masked-self-attention]], each head builds a triangular 512 by 512 score matrix; twelve heads is about 3.1M scores per sequence per block, and [[pretraining-schedule]] runs 64 sequences at a time.

On the choice itself, the paper says only that it largely follows the original [[transformer-gpt1]] work. [[eq-decoder-stack]] treats the block as given, and [[decoder-only-stack]] inherits its interior unchanged. No head-count comparison is reported.

chapters.title: The Sublayer That Holds Two Thirds of the Weights
chapters.body:
The second sublayer is where most of a block's parameters live, and where none of its communication happens.

"Position-wise" in [[position-wise-feedforward-3072]] means the same 768 to 3072 to 768 map runs at every position independently, with nothing passing sideways between them. That splits the block cleanly: attention moves information between tokens, and this sublayer does the per-token computation on what arrived.

Count it. $768 \times 3072$ is 2,359,296, and there are two such matrices, up and back down. About 4.7M, against attention's 2.4M. Two thirds of each block.

Between the two matrices sits [[gelu]], written $x\,\Phi(x)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution. Work two inputs through it. At $x = 2$, $\Phi$ is about 0.977, so the input passes through nearly untouched. At $x = -2$, $\Phi$ is about 0.023, so the output is about $-0.046$ — close to zero, but not zero, and still carrying gradient.

That is the difference from a hard cut at zero. The curve also dips slightly below zero for mildly negative inputs before flattening, so it is not monotone.

The paper states the choice with a citation and no comparison. No ReLU control run appears anywhere in it.

One more thing acts on this sublayer's output. Under [[regularization-setup]], [[residual-embedding-attention-dropout]] applies [[dropout-gpt1]] at rate 0.1 to residual branches, so what a block computes is thinned before it is added back. [[fig-1]] draws the two sublayers in sequence.

chapters.title: One Standard Deviation for Every Matrix
chapters.body:
[[weight-initialization]] draws every weight from $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$. The thing to notice is that this is one number applied to matrices with very different fan-in.

Compare it against the usual scaling. For a projection reading 768 inputs, $1/\sqrt{768}$ is about 0.036, so 0.02 is a little over half of what a fan-in rule would ask. For the feed-forward matrix reading 3072 inputs, $1/\sqrt{3072}$ is about 0.018, and 0.02 is almost exactly it.

So the same draw is roughly fan-in-scaled for the widest matrix in the block and deliberately small for everything else.

The paper's stated reason for getting away with this is [[layer-normalization-gpt1]]. Normalization rescales each position's activations to zero mean and unit variance before applying a learned gain and bias, so the size of what reaches the next matrix is largely reset regardless of how the weights were drawn. The word the paper uses is "sufficient."

That is an assertion, not a result. No initialization sweep is reported, no run that diverged under an alternative, no comparison of any kind.

The prose also does not say where normalization sits within a block, only that it is used extensively throughout the model; the block diagram shows one after each sublayer.

Those learned gains surface again in [[pre-training-optimization]]. The [[decoupled-weight-decay]] term applies $w = 0.01$ to all non-bias and non-gain weights, which exempts them. Together with [[adam-optimizer-gpt1]] and the [[linear-warmup]] over 2000 updates, this is the whole of what keeps early training stable, and none of it is ablated.

chapters.title: The Only Number the Paper Turns
chapters.body:
Every dimension so far arrives as a stated setting with nothing behind it. [[twelve-layer-depth]] is different, because [[layers-transferred]] makes it a variable.

The left panel of [[fig-2]] plots dev accuracy on [[multinli]] and [[race-dataset]] against how many of the twelve pre-trained blocks are carried into fine-tuning. The leftmost point transfers the embedding table alone, which is [[word-embedding-transfer]], and which the paper calls the standard result. From there, accuracy climbs with each block added, reaching up to 9% for full transfer on MultiNLI.

Read what that licenses. The curve is still rising at twelve, and the paper reports no point past it and no run at any other depth.

So the sweep says no transferred layer was dead weight. It does not say twelve was the right depth, and it does not show the gain flattening out.

There is a price attached to the 9%. At roughly 7.1M weights per block, carrying all twelve moves about 85M parameters into the target task, on top of the embedding table.

One nearby number is easy to misread as the same experiment. In [[table-5]], [[ablation-no-pretraining]] costs 14.8 points — but that is the same twelve-layer stack trained on the task from scratch, not the zero-layer end of this curve.

The evidence here is two datasets, dev accuracy, single runs, no error bars.

n-the-corpus-and-the-training-run--shape.title: How the Dimensions Fit Together
n-the-corpus-and-the-training-run--shape.intro: One block, followed from the vector that enters it to the vector that leaves. Then the arithmetic behind the smaller choices the specification states in a sentence each: what each one costs, what it leaves undefined, and how much the paper actually tested.

chapters.title: One Block, Followed Through
chapters.body:
A single position enters a block carrying one [[hidden-state-dimension-768|768-number]] vector. [[input-representation-h0|At layer zero]] that vector is a token embedding plus a position embedding. Above layer zero it is whatever the block below produced.

The attention sublayer first makes three versions of it. The query, key and value projections each multiply the vector by a $768 \times 768$ matrix, so all three come out at full width.

Then the split. Those 768 numbers are cut into [[twelve-attention-heads|twelve]] contiguous slices of 64. Head $h$ takes slice $h$ of the query, slice $h$ of the key and slice $h$ of the value, and never sees the other eleven.

Nothing is duplicated by this. Twelve heads of width 64 cost exactly the arithmetic of one head of width 768. What changes is that the comparison between two tokens becomes twelve separate 64-dimensional dot products rather than one 768-dimensional one — twelve narrow views instead of one wide one.

The head width also fixes the score scale. Attention divides each dot product by $\sqrt{d_k}$, and $d_k = 64$ makes that divisor exactly 8.

Each head's scores then pass the [[masked-self-attention|causal mask]] before the softmax, so positions after the current one get zero weight. There is no encoder output to attend to instead — [[decoder-only-stack|that half is gone]].

The twelve 64-dimensional results are concatenated back to 768 and sent through the fourth $768 \times 768$ matrix.

The second sublayer mixes nothing. [[position-wise-feedforward-3072|The feed-forward network]] runs on each position on its own: up to 3072, activation, back down to 768.

Both sublayers sit on residual branches with [[layer-normalization-gpt1|layer normalization]]. This is the block [[fig-1|Figure 1 draws]] once, stacked twelve times, and written out in [[eq-decoder-stack|Equation 2]] — the [[transformer-gpt1|transformer]] block with the encoder attention removed.

chapters.title: Where the Count Actually Lands
chapters.body:
The total is worth splitting three ways, because the three parts behave differently.

Inside a block the two sublayers are not equal. Attention's four projections come to $4 \times 589{,}824$. The feed-forward pair comes to $2 \times 2{,}359{,}296$, which is that same quantity twice over. So exactly two thirds of a block's weights sit in the position-wise map and one third in attention.

Most of the per-block capacity is the transformation applied after mixing, not the mixing.

The embedding table is the other large piece. [[bpe-merges-40000|40,000 merges]] is not itself a row count: the vocabulary is the base symbols, plus the merged symbols, plus the tokens added later for fine-tuning, and the paper never states the total. Round to 40,000 rows and the table is $40{,}000 \times 768 = 30{,}720{,}000$ parameters.

That table is used at both ends. [[token-embedding-matrix|$W_e$]] maps tokens in at the bottom, and [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings|its transpose scores the vocabulary]] at the top. There is no separate output matrix, so those rows take gradient from the input lookup and from the final softmax together.

Then there is a cost no parameter count shows. Each head builds a score matrix over the [[context-window-512-tokens|512-token window]]: $512 \times 512 = 262{,}144$ numbers. Twelve heads across [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve layers]] make $37{,}748{,}736$ of them for one sequence, and a minibatch holds 64 sequences — about 2.4 billion attention weights alive per step.

In arithmetic it is smaller than that sounds. Per token per block, the four projections are 2.36M multiply-accumulates, the feed-forward 4.72M, and the attend-and-average over 512 positions about 0.79M. At this window the quadratic term is roughly a tenth of the work. The window costs memory more than it costs compute, and none of this appears in [[model-specification|the specification]].

chapters.title: A Table Instead of a Function
chapters.body:
[[learned-position-embeddings|The switch to a learned table]] gets one sentence in the paper and no reason attached to it.

The two options are different kinds of object. A sinusoid is a function of the slot index and the channel: hand it any integer and it returns a vector. Slot 900 has an encoding whether or not any training sequence ever reached slot 900.

A table is a parameter. $W_p$ has 512 rows because the model reads 512 slots. Row 513 is not wrong or degraded. It does not exist.

The window has stopped being a training decision and become a shape.

In parameters it is cheap: $512 \times 768 = 393{,}216$, under half a percent of the stack.

The interesting difference is in training traffic, since a learned row only knows what gradient reached it. [[pretraining-schedule|Every pre-training minibatch]] is 64 contiguous sequences of exactly 512 tokens. Every one of the 512 rows therefore appears once in every sequence, at every update. The last row is trained as hard as the first.

Stage two does not hold that property. [[task-specific-input-transformations|Task inputs are rewritten]] into a single sequence starting at slot one, bracketed by [[start-and-end-tokens|start and end tokens]] and split by a [[delimiter-token|delimiter]]. Many of those sequences stop well short of 512 slots, and fine-tuning runs for [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|three passes]] over a small dataset.

So the high-index rows enter each task carrying only what pre-training put there, and receive little further gradient.

The paper measures none of this. It reports no comparison of learned against sinusoidal embeddings, and no evidence that the substitution changed any result.

chapters.title: A Gate That Slides
chapters.body:
[[gelu|GELU]] and ReLU differ in exactly one factor. ReLU multiplies $x$ by the indicator $\mathbb{1}[x>0]$, a gate that is either 0 or 1. GELU multiplies $x$ by $\Phi(x)$, a gate that slides continuously between them.

Put two numbers through it. At $x = 2$, $\Phi(2) = 0.977$ and the output is $1.95$, where ReLU would give $2$. At $x = -2$, $\Phi(-2) = 0.023$ and the output is $-0.046$, where ReLU would give exactly $0$.

Two things follow from that.

First, there is no flat half-line. ReLU's derivative is identically zero for every negative input, so a unit driven negative receives no gradient at all. GELU's derivative is $\Phi(x) + x\phi(x)$, which shrinks as $x$ falls but is never zero across a stretch.

Second, the function is not monotone. That derivative crosses zero near $x = -0.75$, where GELU bottoms out around $-0.17$ and then climbs back toward zero. Slightly more negative inputs can produce less negative outputs.

All of this happens inside the feed-forward sublayer, between its two matrices.

The evidence behind the choice is thin, and the paper does not pretend otherwise. It names GELU with a citation and says nothing more. It is not among [[ablation-studies|the three removals]] the paper does run — [[ablation-no-pretraining|no pre-training]], [[ablation-lstm-substitution|an LSTM in place of the transformer]], and [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective|no auxiliary loss]] — reported in [[table-5|Table 5]]. Nothing here says what the same stack with ReLU would have scored.

chapters.title: Why 0.02 Was Enough
chapters.body:
The claim attached to [[weight-initialization|$\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$]] is that layernorm made it sufficient. It reads better once you see what would otherwise have gone wrong.

Take a $768 \times 768$ projection whose input components have unit variance. Draw the weights at standard deviation $\sigma$ and the outputs come out at $\sigma\sqrt{768}$, which is $\sigma \times 27.7$.

For that to land at 1, $\sigma$ would have to be $1/\sqrt{768} = 0.036$. The rule usually paired with rectified activations asks for $\sqrt{2/768} = 0.051$. At $0.02$ the output standard deviation is $0.554$ instead.

That is a shrink of nearly half at every matrix. There are two matrix stages per block and twelve blocks in [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder|the stack]]. Compounded, $0.554^{24}$ is about $7 \times 10^{-7}$ — the signal would reach the top essentially gone, and the gradient would come back the same way.

Normalization removes the compounding. Each normalized point rescales its vector to zero mean and unit variance across the 768 channels, so the shrink is undone before the next stage and absolute scale never accumulates.

What the small draw then controls is not activation scale. It is how large each sublayer's contribution is against the residual stream it is added to, and at step zero that is small — further attenuated by [[residual-embedding-attention-dropout|dropout on the residual branches]].

One related detail sits in the same paragraph of the paper: [[decoupled-weight-decay|the modified weight decay]] skips all bias and gain weights, leaving layernorm's learned scales free.

The same 0.02 covers every matrix, with no per-layer adjustment — which is what makes it simple. And "sufficient" is a report that the run worked, not a comparison. No initialization experiment appears in [[pre-training-optimization|the training setup]] or the analysis.

n-from-language-model-to-classifier--why.title: The Second Loss, Term by Term
n-from-language-model-to-classifier--why.intro: The parent settled what the auxiliary term is and where the paper puts it. This level does the arithmetic: which text the loss actually reads, what the tied head saves and what it costs to run, what $\lambda = 0.5$ does and does not pin down, how thin the evidence for the two claimed effects is, and what the ablation row comes to when you do the subtraction yourself.

chapters.title: Which Text the Loss Reads
chapters.body:
$\mathcal{C}$ — the [[labeled-dataset-c]] — does not hold plain sentences by the time either loss touches it. Its inputs have already been through [[task-specific-input-transformations]].

So the sequence the auxiliary term scores is the transformed one, and that sequence contains tokens no book contains. Every input is bracketed by [[start-and-end-tokens]]. The parts inside are separated by the [[delimiter-token]] `$`.

[[eq-lm-objective]] asks the model to predict each token from the tokens before it, and these markers sit in the stream like any other token. The paper does not say whether the positions holding them are scored or skipped.

How many sequences an example produces also varies by task. [[entailment-input-transformation]] makes one sequence from a premise and a hypothesis. [[similarity-input-transformation]] makes two, one for each ordering of the pair. [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]] makes one per candidate answer, so a four-way multiple-choice question yields four.

Whatever the label loss reads, the auxiliary term reads exactly the same sequences.

What it never reads is the label. $y$ is not in the token stream at all; it is reachable only through [[linear-output-layer-wy]]. So the gradient from the auxiliary term flows into the embeddings and into every transformer block, and never into $W_y$.

There is a shift in the text itself as well. Pre-training scored [[long-range-contiguous-text]] in windows of [[context-window-512-tokens]]. A premise, a `$` and a hypothesis is a much shorter object with a marker in the middle.

The same objective is now being maximized on text of a different shape, and the paper does not comment on that.

chapters.title: Free in Parameters, Not in Compute
chapters.body:
"No new parameters" is worth putting a number on.

The vocabulary comes from [[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1]] built with [[bpe-merges-40000]], so it holds on the order of 40,000 subword units. Each state in the stack is [[hidden-state-dimension-768]] wide. A projection from a 768-dimensional state to 40,000 scores is therefore a matrix of about 30.7 million entries.

[[output-softmax-tied-embeddings]] means that matrix is never stored. The head is the transpose of [[token-embedding-matrix]], which the input side needs anyway.

For scale: each of the [[twelve-layer-depth]] blocks holds roughly 7 million weights, so twelve of them come to around 85 million. An untied output projection would have added about a third of the stack again, carried through pre-training and into every fine-tuning run.

That is what the count in [[minimal-extra-parameters]] — one matrix $W_y$, plus embeddings for delimiters — quietly rests on. It is also the same measure the paper uses against [[per-task-parameter-cost]] elsewhere.

Parameters are not the only cost. $W_y$ is applied once per sequence, at [[final-token-activation]]. The tied head is applied at every position, and each application is those 30.7 million multiply-adds followed by a softmax over 40,000 rows.

A pass through all twelve blocks at one position is around 85 million multiply-adds, before counting attention. So scoring every position with the language modelling head adds roughly a third to the forward work of a fine-tuning step.

Under [[three-epochs-fine-tuning]] at [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch]] that is a bounded amount of extra compute. The paper reports no timing for either configuration.

chapters.title: What $\lambda = 0.5$ Balances
chapters.body:
Both terms in [[eq-combined-objective]] are written as sums, and they sum over different things.

[[supervised-objective-l2]], as written in [[eq-supervised-objective]], contributes one log-probability per labelled example: the log-probability of that example's correct label. [[language-modeling-objective]], applied to the same example, contributes one log-probability per token.

Take a premise-hypothesis pair forty tokens long. The label side of the sum has one term in it. The auxiliary side has forty. Scaling by [[auxiliary-objective-weight]] at $0.5$ leaves twenty against one.

So $0.5$ does not, on its own, mean the two objectives are weighted evenly. Where the ratio actually lands depends on whether an implementation sums or averages each term, and on how long the task's sequences are. The paper writes sums, and does not say which its code does.

One consequence is that a single $\lambda$ means different things across the twelve datasets. A [[race-dataset]] example is a passage, a question and a candidate answer. A [[cola]] example is one sentence. At the same $\lambda$, the auxiliary term carries far more of the gradient in the first case than in the second.

$\lambda$ is reported once, in the closing line of [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]], in the same list as the learning rate, the batch size and the [[classifier-dropout]]. One value covers every task. No search over it is reported, and no sensitivity is measured.

That matters more here than it would for a well-behaved knob. The ablation ahead reports the term's effect changing sign from dataset to dataset, which makes a per-task $\lambda$ the obvious response — and it is not attempted.

chapters.title: Two Claims, Unequally Evidenced
chapters.body:
The paper's case for keeping the term is one sentence: including language modelling as an auxiliary objective helped by improving generalization of the supervised model, and by accelerating convergence. Two references follow, cited as prior work that saw the same.

The two claims are not evidenced the same way, so take them apart.

Generalization is testable inside this paper. Train with the term, train without it, compare held-out scores. That experiment exists — it is [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]], one of the three in [[ablation-studies]] — and the next chapter reads it.

Convergence has nothing measuring it. No fine-tuning learning curve appears anywhere in the paper. [[fig-2]] holds the only training-progress plots, and both concern stage one: the left panel is [[layers-transferred]], the right tracks [[zero-shot-behaviors]] across pre-training updates.

Neither says how many fine-tuning steps a run took with the term compared to without. The claim is stated and left there.

No mechanism is offered for either effect. The paper does not say whether the term acts as a regularizer, keeps the tied head calibrated on text of the new shape, or does something else. [[pretraining-as-regularization]] is raised in the related work, but about stage one, not about this.

The cited corroboration also sits at a slant. The clearer of the two references, named under [[auxiliary-training-objectives]], added a language modelling loss to sequence labelling — predicting a tag at every token, not one label from the last position.

And the paper's own reading of that branch is that [[generative-pretraining]] already learns several of the linguistic aspects such an objective would supply. That is an argument for the term mattering less here than it did there.

chapters.title: Doing the Subtraction Yourself
chapters.body:
[[table-5]] carries a row labelled "Transformer w/o aux LM". It is the same recipe with $\lambda$ set to zero.

Start with what it does not cover. The table reports eight datasets, not twelve. [[snli]], [[scitail]], RACE and the [[story-cloze-test]] are absent — so the term's effect on the two benchmarks carrying the paper's largest reported margins is never measured at all.

Now the eight. Keeping the term costs 2.5 points on CoLA (45.4 against 47.9), 0.7 on [[sst-2]] (91.3 against 92.0), 2.6 on [[mrpc]] (82.3 against 84.9) and 1.2 on [[sts-b]] (82.0 against 83.2).

It gains 0.5 on [[qqp]] (70.3 against 69.8), 0.7 on [[multinli]] (81.8 against 81.1), 1.2 on [[qnli]] (88.1 against 86.9) and 1.6 on [[rte]] (56.0 against 54.4).

The losses total 7.0 points. The gains total 4.0. Net $-3.0$ across eight datasets is $-0.375$ each, which rounds to the gap between the two reported averages, 74.7 and 75.0.

That average is unweighted, and the caption says so. It adds one Matthews correlation, four accuracies, two F1 scores and one Pearson correlation as though they shared a unit. CoLA's 2.5-point Matthews swing counts exactly as much as QQP's 0.5-point F1 swing.

Then the size reading. RTE is a dataset the paper itself calls one of the smaller ones, at 2490 examples, and it shows the largest single gain from keeping the term.

STS-B, at roughly 5.7k examples, is hurt by it and fits the trend. Those two are the only ones of the eight whose sizes the paper prints.

n-one-sequence-per-task--the-four-shapes.title: Four Shapes, and What Each Costs to Run
n-one-sequence-per-task--the-four-shapes.intro: The parent priced the four templates. This level takes each apart at the level of the mechanism: what the markers actually add in the cases that look free, why the similarity merge is addition rather than something else, what the softmax over candidates is normalizing, and where the running bill lands against a window the paper never budgets for.

chapters.title: The Two Templates That Only Add Markers
chapters.body:
Calling the classification case untransformed is nearly right, and the exception is worth having. The paper says all transformations include adding randomly initialized start and end tokens, $\langle s\rangle$ and $\langle e\rangle$ ([[start-and-end-tokens]]).

So a single sentence going into [[text-classification]] is still rewritten. Two positions are bracketed onto it, and both carry embeddings that did not exist during pre-training.

Those embeddings are learned during fine-tuning. They belong to the small set of freshly initialized parameters that a new task brings with it ([[minimal-extra-parameters]]).

Entailment adds one more symbol. The [[delimiter-token]] `$` goes between the premise and the hypothesis ([[entailment-input-transformation]]), so the sequence has five parts: start, premise, delimiter, hypothesis, end. One forward pass, over a sequence of length $|p| + |h| + 3$.

The order in that sequence is not a choice anyone made. [[natural-language-inference]] hands over a directed pair: the premise is given, and the hypothesis is the thing being judged against it.

That direction interacts with the stack in a way the paper does not comment on. Under [[masked-self-attention]] each position attends only to itself and to earlier positions.

Hypothesis tokens can therefore attend back into the premise. Premise tokens cannot see the hypothesis at all.

The premise is read once, without knowing what will be asked of it. Only the hypothesis is read in the light of the other sentence.

[[fig-1]] draws these two panels as nearly the same picture: one text block for classification, two blocks and a delimiter for entailment, each feeding one transformer and one linear head. That visual sameness is the [[traversal-style-approach]] working on its easy cases, where [[structured-inputs]] already carry a reading order and only need writing down in it.

chapters.title: Buying Symmetry with a Second Pass
chapters.body:
The repair fits in one sentence of the paper: build both orderings, process each independently, add the two representations element-wise, feed the sum to the linear layer ([[similarity-input-transformation]]).

Walk the shapes. Each pass produces $h_l^m$, the top block's activation at the last position ([[final-token-activation]]), which is a vector of 768 numbers in the trained model ([[model-specification]]).

Two passes give two such vectors. Adding them gives one vector of 768 numbers, which is exactly the input [[linear-output-layer-wy]] already expected ([[eq-task-head]]).

So the head is not told it is being fed a sum. Its shape is identical to the entailment case.

Addition is doing one specific job here. Write the stack as $f$ and the two sentences as $a$ and $b$. The quantity $f([a;b]) + f([b;a])$ is unchanged when you relabel which sentence was called first, because addition commutes.

Concatenating the two vectors would also use both orderings. But it would keep a slot meaning "the pass where $a$ came first", widening the head's input to 1536 and putting the arbitrary choice straight back in. Averaging would serve as well as addition, differing by a factor of two that $W_y$ can absorb. The paper names addition and does not compare the alternatives.

Be precise about what became symmetric. Each summand is still produced by an order-sensitive traversal; only the aggregate is invariant. That is sufficient, because the prediction is a function of the aggregate alone.

The price is two forward and two backward passes per example, paid on [[mrpc]], [[qqp]] and [[sts-b]] ([[semantic-similarity]]) across all three fine-tuning epochs ([[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]]). No ablation isolates the symmetric sum, so what it contributes to those three scores is not measured.

chapters.title: When the Number of Answers Is Not Known in Advance
chapters.body:
Question answering breaks the pattern somewhere else. Entailment had a fixed number of parts; here the part count is a property of the individual example.

The template is $[z; q; \$; a_k]$, built once per candidate ([[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]]). Read the punctuation closely. There is one delimiter, and it sits between the question and the answer.

The passage and the question are run together with no marker at their join. The prose agrees — concatenate the document context and question with each possible answer, delimiter in between — and the multiple-choice panel of the figure draws a single Delim box.

Why not keep one sequence and give the head one output column per option? Because the option count moves. The [[story-cloze-test]] offers two endings ([[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning]]). [[race-dataset]] is built from middle and high school exam passages, and the paper never prints how many choices those questions carry.

A matrix with a column per option would fix that number when the model is built. Running the same [[decoder-only-stack]] $K$ times instead moves the count out of the architecture and into a loop. Handling variable structure inside the network is what [[task-specific-architectures]] would do, and that is the thing being declined.

The $K$ scores are then normalized by a softmax across sequences. The label space is assembled at run time from whatever candidates the example supplied.

The head's shape is not stated. The figure draws a Linear box after each candidate's pass, and for a distribution over $K$ options to come out, each box must emit one number, which makes $W_y$ a $768 \times 1$ matrix.

Whether one such matrix is shared across candidates is left unsaid. A separate matrix per slot would make a candidate's score depend on its position in the list, which is the dependence this design works elsewhere to remove.

The supervised loss ([[eq-supervised-objective]]) is the log-probability of the correct candidate, so the $K$ passes touch each other only through the shared normalizer. [[table-3]] reports what comes out.

chapters.title: The Bill, and the One Limit Nobody Prices
chapters.body:
Add the passes up per training example. Classification, one. Entailment, one. Similarity, two. Multiple choice, $K$.

This is a multiplier on fine-tuning compute and on activation memory. It is not a multiplier on parameters: the same weights run every time, which is the whole point of [[task-specific-input-transformations]] and of the [[task-agnostic-model]] claim ([[table-1]]).

It is also a multiplier on the cheaper of the two stages. Pre-training runs 100 epochs over minibatches of 64 sequences; fine-tuning runs three epochs at batch size 32. Doubling or quadrupling the short stage is a small addition to the total, though the paper never states the comparison itself.

Now the limit. The stack reads 512 tokens ([[context-window-512-tokens]]), a number set during pre-training, where the objective conditions each token on a window of that size ([[language-modeling-objective]]). Position information comes from a trained matrix with one vector per slot ([[learned-position-embeddings]]), so there are no vectors for positions beyond the last one pre-training used.

A comprehension sequence has to fit a whole passage, a question, an answer and the markers inside that. Tokenization pushes the other way: byte-pair encoding with 40,000 merges ([[byte-pair-encoding-gpt1]], part of the [[text-preprocessing-pipeline]]) splits rare words into several units, so the token count runs above the word count.

The paper does not say whether long passages are truncated, or from which end.

The silence sits oddly next to the argument being made. RACE is chosen partly for having more reasoning-type questions than [[cnn-and-squad-contrast]], and is described as a fitting test for a model trained on [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1]]. Long range is being claimed as the strength, while the mechanism that would bound it goes unmentioned.

This is a gap in the reporting, not a demonstrated fault. The RACE numbers were obtained somehow; the paper just does not say how the input was made to fit.

n-the-scoreboard--the-margins.title: The Numbers Behind the Margins
n-the-scoreboard--the-margins.intro: The parent laid the figures out. This level says what each dataset is actually asking a system to do, what kind of system held the number being subtracted from, and where a blended figure like RACE's 59.0 comes from arithmetically.

chapters.title: What Entailment Asks, and How It Is Fed In
chapters.body:
All five columns of [[table-2]] score the same task. A system reads two sentences, a premise and a hypothesis, and assigns one of three labels: the premise entails the hypothesis, contradicts it, or leaves it undecided. That is [[natural-language-inference]], which the paper also calls recognizing textual entailment.

Section 4.2 names what makes it hard, and the list is worth reading slowly.

Lexical entailment: knowing that one word licenses another, so that a cat on a mat entails an animal on a mat. [[coreference]]: two expressions referring to the same entity, so that whether a pronoun points at the premise's subject or its object can flip the label. Lexical and syntactic ambiguity: a word with two senses, or a phrase that could attach in two places.

None of that is built into the network. Whatever the model has of it, it has from predicting next tokens on books.

The feed is identical across all five datasets. Premise tokens and hypothesis tokens are concatenated with a `$` [[delimiter-token]] between them — the [[entailment-input-transformation]] — and the sequence is bracketed by [[start-and-end-tokens]]. The [[final-token-activation]] from the top block goes through [[linear-output-layer-wy]] and softmaxes into three label scores.

So nothing is reshaped per column. There is no per-dataset [[task-specific-architectures|architecture]] tuned against that benchmark's quirks.

That matters for reading the spread. A gain of 5.8 points on one column and 0.6 on another came out of the same weights and the same [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|three epochs of fine-tuning]]. Whatever explains the difference sits in the datasets, and in who held the previous number.

chapters.title: Five Sources, Five Different Ceilings
chapters.body:
Where the sentences come from differs by column, and the paper picks the five for exactly that spread.

[[snli]] pairs are written over image captions, so its premises describe scenes. [[multinli]] mixes transcribed speech, popular fiction and government reports. [[qnli]] is built over Wikipedia articles. [[scitail]] is derived from science exam questions. [[rte]] is drawn from news.

MultiNLI's two reported columns follow from that mix. The matched development set is drawn from genres that also appear in its training data. The mismatched set is drawn from genres held out of training. Mismatched is the lower score for nearly every system in the table, which is why 82.1 and 81.4 sit apart rather than on top of each other.

Size differs as much as source. SNLI is the largest dataset in the whole evaluation at roughly 550k training pairs. RTE is the smallest at 2,490.

Now the other side of each subtraction. SNLI's 89.3 came from five-model ensembles, one of them ESIM — a biLSTM built for inference — with [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] features added as inputs. That column has absorbed a lot of task-specific work.

QNLI is the opposite case. Of the [[baseline-comparisons]] in the table, only the two multi-task models taken from the [[glue-benchmark]] paper report a QNLI number at all; the rest of the column is dashes. Its 82.3 comes from a general multi-task system, not from something built and re-tuned for QNLI across several papers.

So the two figures are not measuring the same contest. 0.6 is taken off a column many groups have pushed on. 5.8 is taken off a column almost nobody had entered.

chapters.title: Why RACE, and What Its Two Splits Say
chapters.body:
[[race-dataset|RACE]] is picked with a stated reason, and the reason is part of the evidence.

It is reading comprehension assembled from English exam passages, middle school and high school, each with multiple-choice questions written to test whether a student understood the passage. It is the larger half of the [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning]] family.

The argument for choosing it runs through [[cnn-and-squad-contrast|CNN and SQuAD]]. On those, the answer is something located in the passage — a span, or an entity filling a blank. RACE, the paper says, has been shown to contain more reasoning-type questions than either, which makes it "the perfect evaluation for our model which is trained to handle long-range contexts".

Read that plainly. The benchmark is selected because it suits the property being claimed, and the claim about its question mix is cited to other work rather than measured here.

Each candidate answer is scored on its own. Document, question and that one answer are concatenated into a single sequence, and the resulting scores are normalized across candidates by a softmax — the [[qa-and-commonsense-input-transformation]]. Passage plus question plus answer is a long input, which is where [[bookscorpus]] and its [[long-range-contiguous-text]] are meant to pay off.
