The split arithmetic is checkable. The model's two splits are 62.9 and 57.4, whose midpoint is 60.15, yet the combined figure in [[table-3]] is 59.0 — below that midpoint, nearer the high-school number.

Solving $62.9 - 5.5w = 59.0$ gives $w \approx 0.71$. About seven in ten RACE test questions are high-school ones.

Run the same sum on the previous best row, where 60.2 and 50.3 combine to 53.3, and $w \approx 0.70$. The two rows agree, which is a small check that the combined column is a weighted blend and nothing stranger.

chapters.title: Story Cloze, and the Reading Laid Over It
chapters.body:
[[story-cloze-test|Story Cloze]] hands over a short multi-sentence story and two candidate endings, and asks which one actually finishes it.

Two options means chance is 50. The live range on that column is not 0 to 100 but 50 to 100. A system at 77.6 has covered a little over half the distance from guessing to perfect; 86.5 covers about three quarters of it.

The input format is the one RACE gets. Each ending is appended to the story to make its own sequence, both sequences are scored, and the two scores are normalized against each other. [[supervised-fine-tuning]] on the labelled endings trains the single linear layer sitting on top.

The previous 77.6 is a single system, the Hidden Coherence Model, not an ensemble.

The paper reads 77.6 against 86.5, together with RACE, as showing the model handles [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|long-range context]] well. There is a mechanism behind that reading: attention over the whole context is argued to give a more [[transformer-inductive-bias|structured memory]] than a recurrent state carried forward, and the paper elsewhere points at an [[lstm-short-range-limitation|LSTM's shorter effective range]].

But note what the two numbers do not do. Neither column varies story length, or context length, or anything else that would isolate range as the cause.

A model that had simply absorbed more [[world-knowledge]] about how situations usually end would move that number in the same direction by the same amount.

The interpretation is laid over the result. It is consistent with the result. It is not separated out by it.

chapters.title: The Same Margins as Error Reduction
chapters.body:
Every margin so far is a subtraction in accuracy points, which is what the paper means by [[absolute-improvement]]. That treatment gives a point gained at 89 the same weight as a point gained at 53.

Here are the same rows read a second way: what share of the previous system's errors disappeared. This re-expression is not in the paper.

SNLI. The old 89.3 leaves $100 - 89.3 = 10.7$ points of error, and 89.9 leaves 10.1. The gain removes $0.6 / 10.7 \approx 5.6\%$ of them.

MultiNLI matched: $1.5 / 19.4 \approx 7.7\%$. Mismatched: $1.3 / 19.9 \approx 6.5\%$.

SciTail: $5.0 / 16.7 \approx 30\%$. QNLI: $5.8 / 17.7 \approx 33\%$. Story Cloze: $8.9 / 22.4 \approx 40\%$.

RACE overall: $5.7 / 46.7 \approx 12\%$, because that column starts with nearly half its questions wrong.

The RACE splits move closer together under this reading. High school clears $7.1 / 49.7 \approx 14\%$ of its errors, middle school $2.7 / 39.8 \approx 7\%$ — still twice as much, but not the 2.6-fold gap the raw points suggest.

This second reading is not neutral either. Near a ceiling, some of the remaining errors are label noise rather than failures a better model could fix, so a small relative gain up there may be worth more than it looks.

Neither reading settles which win is largest. What the paper banks instead is a count: [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12]] across the [[evaluation-task-families]], one [[task-agnostic-model]] behind every entry, and the count treats all nine alike.

Nothing in these two tables says why the wins happened. That argument is made separately, by [[layers-transferred]] in [[fig-2]] and by [[ablation-no-pretraining]].

n-which-parts-do-the-work--three-removal.title: Three Removals, Eight Datasets
n-which-parts-do-the-work--three-removal.intro: The level above gave the three headline deltas and the shape of the grid. This one puts every cell on the page, does the additions the table only prints the results of, and asks what each row can and cannot license.

chapters.title: What the Average Column Is Adding Up
chapters.body:
Start with the reference row of [[table-5]], left to right: 45.4, 91.3, 82.3, 82.0, 70.3, 81.8, 88.1, 56.0.

Add them and you get 597.2. Divide by eight and you get 74.65, which the table prints as 74.7.

That is the whole operation. Nothing is rescaled first, and no dataset is weighted by how many training examples it has.

The eight columns do not share a zero. Matthews correlation on [[cola]] sits at 0 for a classifier that guesses, so its usable range runs from 0 to 100. Accuracy on [[sst-2]] sits near 50 for a coin flip on a binary label, and near 33 on three-way [[multinli]]. F1 on the positive class rewards a model that simply answers yes when most pairs carry the positive label, so the floor for [[mrpc]] sits high rather than at zero.

Four different floors, averaged as if they were one scale.

The practical effect is not that the average is meaningless. It is that the gaps between rows are set mostly by the columns with the most room to move, and those are the ones whose metric bottoms out at zero.

One more thing about the grid itself. Each of the three lower rows removes exactly one component from the top row, and no row removes two. There is no run with an [[lstm-gpt1]] and no pre-training, and none with neither pre-training nor the auxiliary loss.

So the table reports three separate effects measured against one reference, and nothing in it measures how they interact.

A last caution on the number. These eight are the [[glue-benchmark]] tasks, but 74.7 is not the 72.8 GLUE score reported in [[table-4]]. They are different quantities and should not be read against each other.

chapters.title: Where the 14.8 Actually Comes From
chapters.body:
The [[ablation-no-pretraining]] row reads 18.9, 84.0, 79.4, 30.9, 65.5, 75.7, 71.2, 53.8. That sums to 479.4, and $479.4 / 8 = 59.925$, printed as 59.9.

The headline 14.8 is the difference of two rounded numbers. Unrounded it is $74.65 - 59.925 = 14.725$.

Now take the drops column by column. CoLA falls 26.5. SST-2 falls 7.3. [[mrpc]] falls 2.9. STS-B falls from 82.0 to 30.9, which is 51.1. [[qqp]] falls 4.8, [[multinli|MNLI]] 6.1, [[qnli]] 16.9, and RTE 2.2.

Those eight drops sum to 117.8, and $117.8 / 8 = 14.7$, which is the gap.

STS-B alone contributes $51.1 / 8 = 6.4$ of it. CoLA contributes 3.3 and QNLI 2.1. Three columns therefore account for 11.8 of the 14.7.

The remaining five columns together contribute 2.9. Five of the eight datasets move less, in total, than STS-B moves on its own.

Why STS-B in particular. It is the smallest training set in the evaluation at roughly 5.7k pairs, its target is a continuous similarity score, and its metric is Pearson correlation, whose chance value is 0. Fine-tuning is [[three-epochs-fine-tuning]] at [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch]], so from a random initialization that is a few hundred updates on a regression target.

At the other end, RTE moves 2.2 points on 2490 training examples, with both values close to where a majority-class predictor would sit.

The paper's sentence is that the lack of [[generative-pretraining]] hurts across all the tasks. Every column is down, so the claim holds exactly as written.

The spread runs from 2.2 to 51.1, so "across the board" describes the direction and not the size. The average is largely two columns of [[labeled-data-scarcity]] showing up at once.

chapters.title: The LSTM Row Changes More Than One Thing
chapters.body:
The [[ablation-lstm-substitution]] row reads 30.3, 90.5, 83.2, 71.8, 68.1, 73.7, 81.1, 54.6. That is 553.3, and $553.3 / 8 = 69.16$, printed 69.1.

The per-column gaps against the full model are 15.1 on CoLA, 0.8 on SST-2, minus 0.9 on MRPC, 10.2 on STS-B, 2.2 on [[qqp]], 8.1 on [[multinli|MNLI]], 7.0 on QNLI and 1.4 on RTE.

CoLA and STS-B again supply 3.2 of the 5.6. The same two columns that dominate the pre-training row dominate this one.

Now the substituted model. It is one recurrent layer of 2048 units. The [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder]] it replaces is [[twelve-layer-depth]] of blocks at [[hidden-state-dimension-768]], each carrying a [[position-wise-feedforward-3072]] inner layer, as fixed by the [[model-specification]].

Depth goes from twelve to one. Width per position goes from 768 to 2048. The mechanism for mixing information across positions changes from attention to a gated recurrent state.

Three changes, one number.

There is also a missing measurement. The paper reports its transformer's [[token-level-perplexity]] of 18.4 on [[bookscorpus]], and reports nothing equivalent for the LSTM.

So we cannot tell whether the LSTM transferred worse from a comparable language model, or was simply a worse language model before fine-tuning began.

The row also keeps the auxiliary loss switched on, and no LSTM row exists without it.

The [[mrpc]] exception is worth stating precisely. The LSTM's 83.2 beats the full model's 82.3, and it is the only cell in the table where that happens. It does not take the column, because 84.9 elsewhere in the table is higher.

The architecture argument leans on a second, separate observation in [[fig-2]], where the LSTM's zero-shot scores swing more from checkpoint to checkpoint. The paper offers that as [[transformer-inductive-bias]], and it is a different kind of evidence than the 5.6.

chapters.title: The Row That Scores Against the Recipe
chapters.body:
The [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] row reads 47.9, 92.0, 84.9, 83.2, 69.8, 81.1, 86.9, 54.4. That is 600.2, and $600.2 / 8 = 75.025$, printed 75.0.

Split the eight columns by which side wins. Dropping the loss gains 2.5 on CoLA, 0.7 on SST-2, 2.6 on [[mrpc]] and 1.2 on STS-B, for 7.0 points in total.

Keeping it gains 0.5 on [[qqp]], 0.7 on [[multinli|MNLI]], 1.2 on QNLI and 1.6 on [[rte]], for 4.0 points in total.

That is four columns each way. The three tenths on the average come from the size of the margins rather than from winning more columns: $(7.0 - 4.0)/8 = 0.375$.

The paper reads the split by dataset size, and for three of the four columns the reading works. QQP and MNLI have hundreds of thousands of training pairs, QNLI has around a hundred thousand, and all three favour keeping [[auxiliary-lm-objective]].

RTE does not fit. It has 2490 examples, the smallest count among the eight, and it favours keeping the loss by the largest margin of the four.

The paper writes that the trend suggests larger datasets benefit. With four columns on that side and one of them a counterexample, the hedge is doing real work.

The other missing measurement is the weight itself. [[eq-combined-objective]] scales the language modelling term by $\lambda$ against [[supervised-objective-l2]], and [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] fixes [[auxiliary-objective-weight]] at 0.5.

The table contains $\lambda = 0.5$ and $\lambda = 0$. Two points, no curve, and no run at 0.25 or 1.0.

The ordering matters too. Every number in [[table-2]] and [[table-3]], across the full [[evaluation-task-families]], was produced at $\lambda = 0.5$.

So this row reports on a setting already committed to, rather than choosing one.

n-the-mismatch--two-questions--machinery.title: Three Kinds of Machinery, Three Kinds of Cost
n-the-mismatch--two-questions--machinery.intro: The parent named three fine-tuning-side mechanisms and priced them in a phrase each. This level takes them apart: what the per-task network is actually made of, what a staged schedule costs when you count runs instead of weights, what the second loss costs once you notice the head it reuses — and then the one number the paper puts on the only one of the three it keeps.

chapters.title: The Network You Build Once Per Task
chapters.body:
Start with what the alternative is physically made of.

You hold a pre-trained representation. For entailment you put it at the bottom of a stack. Above it you place a module that reads two sequences at once: an attention layer that lets every hypothesis token look at every premise token, then a pooling step that collapses the resulting matrix to a vector, then a classifier on that vector. For single-sentence classification you skip the cross-attention and keep a pooling scheme. That upper module is what the paper calls [[task-specific-architectures]].

It costs twice.

First in design. Someone decides that entailment wants cross-attention and that classification wants max-pooling rather than mean-pooling, and those decisions are made per task by hand.

Second in weights. The module is initialized fresh and trained on the task's labels alone. It never sees raw text. Section 3.3 states the consequence plainly: such an approach "re-introduces a significant amount of task-specific customization and does not use [[transfer-learning]] for these additional architectural components."

So transfer stops at the seam between the pre-trained part and the hand-built part. The paper's way of counting that is [[per-task-parameter-cost]] — how many freshly initialized parameters a new task needs.

The replacement absorbs the same difference somewhere else. [[task-specific-input-transformations]] takes [[structured-inputs]] and, by the [[traversal-style-approach]], writes their parts into one ordered token sequence: [[start-and-end-tokens]] bracket it, a [[delimiter-token]] marks where one part stops. [[fig-1]] draws all four shapes side by side.

What remains to be added on top is then [[linear-output-layer-wy]] plus embeddings for the delimiters — the whole of [[minimal-extra-parameters]], and the basis of the [[task-agnostic-model]] claim.

chapters.title: Schedule, Not Parameters
chapters.body:
The second mechanism costs nothing you can count in a parameter table.

[[ulmfit]] sits inside [[lm-pretraining-then-finetuning-predecessors]], the line the related-work section calls closest to this paper's own, alongside [[semi-supervised-sequence-learning]]. Its fine-tuning is staged. Layers are unfrozen in a chosen order across epochs. Each layer gets its own learning rate. The rate over training follows a shaped curve rather than a plain decay.

Every one of those is a number, and every number has to be found on the task you are fine-tuning. The cost is measured in runs, not in weights.

Set that against what this paper actually did. [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] says: reuse the pre-training settings unless stated otherwise. [[pre-training-optimization]] peaked at $2.5\times10^{-4}$; [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch]] uses $6.25\times10^{-5}$, which is that peak divided by four, with batch size 32. [[three-epochs-fine-tuning]] reports three passes sufficed for most datasets. [[classifier-dropout]] adds dropout at 0.1 on the added head.

[[fine-tuning-lr-schedule]] warms the rate up over the first 0.2% of updates, then decays it linearly to zero. Walk that. A 100,000-example set at batch 32 gives 3,125 updates an epoch, so 9,375 across three epochs, so warmup covers roughly nineteen of them. It is a brief ramp off zero, not a stage.

And no layer is ever frozen. All twelve blocks update from the first step.

Two hedges are in the paper's own wording: "unless specified" and "for most tasks." Some datasets got other settings, and which ones is not reported.

Note also that the paper's stated objection to this same family in related work is [[lstm-short-range-limitation]] — an argument about architecture, not about schedule.

chapters.title: What a Second Loss Actually Costs Here
chapters.body:
The third mechanism is the branch of [[semi-supervised-learning-for-nlp]] the related-work section files under [[auxiliary-training-objectives]]: instead of using unlabelled data to pick a starting point, add an unsupervised term to the supervised loss and optimize the sum.

This paper's instance is [[auxiliary-lm-objective]], written out in [[eq-combined-objective]] as

$$L_3(\mathcal{C}) = L_2(\mathcal{C}) + \lambda\, L_1(\mathcal{C}).$$

Read the argument, not just the symbols. Both terms take $\mathcal{C}$, the labelled task set. The language modelling loss during [[supervised-fine-tuning]] is computed on the task's own inputs, scored simply as text — not on the pre-training corpus. So nothing new has to be loaded.

The two terms score the same example at different granularities. [[supervised-objective-l2]] contributes one log-probability per example, for its label. [[language-modeling-objective]] contributes one per token of that example.

Now the price. A second loss usually implies a second output head. Here it does not, because the language modelling head is the tied embedding matrix $W_e^{\top}$ from [[output-softmax-tied-embeddings]], which is still sitting there from stage one. Parameter cost: zero.

What remains is compute — a softmax over the 40,000-merge subword vocabulary at every position, and its backward pass — and one number, [[auxiliary-objective-weight]], set to 0.5. That value is stated in the setup, not derived, and no sweep over it is reported.

The paper gives two reasons for including the term: better generalization of the supervised model, and faster convergence. Both are reported as things they found, with no mechanism offered, and with prior work cited as having seen the same.

chapters.title: The One Measurement, and What It Covers
chapters.body:
[[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] is the row in [[table-5]] that tests the mechanism this paper kept. Fine-tune without the language modelling term, hold everything else fixed.

The average score goes up by 0.3.

Sit with the direction. The one mechanism of the three that survives into the recipe is the one whose removal costs nothing on the aggregate number the paper itself reports.

It earns its place unevenly. The term helps on [[qqp]] and on the [[natural-language-inference]] sets, and the paper reads the pattern as larger datasets benefiting while smaller ones do not.

Two limits on how far that reading carries. Size is not a controlled variable here; it is a trend read off a handful of columns whose training sets run from roughly 550k examples on [[snli]] down to 2,490 on [[rte]]. And RTE is both an NLI set and the smallest of them, so the paper's two summaries — helps on NLI, helps on large data — do not pick out quite the same columns. Separately, $\lambda$ stayed at 0.5 throughout, so the comparison is 0.5 against 0, not a curve.

Put the magnitude next to its neighbours in the same table. [[ablation-no-pretraining]] costs 14.8 points. [[ablation-lstm-substitution]] costs 5.6. This one gains 0.3 the other way. Inside [[ablation-studies]] it places a distant third.

One last thing the table does not do. It removes parts of this paper's own recipe. Against the per-task network and the staged schedule the paper offers a design argument and a scoreboard — not an ablation row.

n-the-corpus-and-the-training-run--shape.title: Two Sublayers, One at a Time
n-the-corpus-and-the-training-run--shape.intro: The parent walked a vector through the block from the outside. This level goes inside the two sublayers separately: what one 64-wide head actually computes and why its divisor is 8, what the mask does arithmetically and why the training objective requires it, where the residual branches and the normalization sit around each sublayer, and what it costs that the feed-forward network applies the same map at every position.

chapters.title: Inside One Head
chapters.body:
Take head seven, at position $i$, in the middle of some block.

Its query is not the full vector. It is slice seven: sixty-four of the [[hidden-state-dimension-768|768]] numbers the query projection produced. The key it compares against, at some earlier position $j$, is slice seven of that position's key vector — the same sixty-four coordinates, never any of the others.

The score is their dot product. Sixty-four products, summed into one scalar.

Do that for every ordered pair and you have a grid of scalars, one per pair, for each of the [[twelve-attention-heads|twelve heads]] in each of the twelve blocks. With a [[context-window-512-tokens|512-token window]] that is $512 \times 512$ entries per head.

Now the divisor. Suppose the query and key entries are roughly independent, near zero mean, near unit scale. A sum of sixty-four such products has variance about sixty-four, so a typical score sits around $\pm 8$ — and scores of that size push the softmax towards putting nearly all its weight on one position, where its gradient is close to flat. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ pulls the scores back to order one.

So the divisor tracks head width, not model width. Six heads of 128 would have divided by about 11.3 instead.

After the softmax, the weights multiply the value slices — again sixty-four numbers each — and the head emits sixty-four numbers.

The paper does not derive any of this. Its [[model-specification|setup paragraph]] gives the head count and the state size in one sentence, and says the [[multi-layer-transformer-decoder|decoder]] largely follows the original [[transformer-gpt1|transformer]] for the rest.

chapters.title: What the Mask Is Actually Doing
chapters.body:
The mask is addition, not deletion.

Before the softmax, every score at a pair where $j > i$ has $-\infty$ added to it — in practice a large negative constant. The softmax exponentiates, $e^{-\infty} = 0$, and those positions come out at exactly zero weight.

The ordering matters. Because the masking happens before normalization, the surviving weights are renormalized over the visible prefix alone and still sum to one. Zeroing weights after a softmax would instead leave each row summing to less than one, by an amount that depends on how far along the sequence the row sits.

Why pay for this at all? Because of how the [[language-modeling-objective|training loss]] is collected. [[eq-lm-objective|Equation 1]] sums a log-probability over every token in the corpus, and one forward pass over a 512-token sequence produces all 512 of those terms at once — 512 predictions, 512 loss terms, one pass.

That density is only sound if each position is blind to its own target. Position $i$ is asked to predict token $i+1$. Unmasked, it could attend to position $i+1$ and read the answer out of that position's value vector, and the loss would fall to nothing while the model learned nothing.

So the score grid is triangular, and roughly half the scores computed are discarded. Position 1 attends to one token; position 512 attends to 512.

There is also nothing else for a head to attend to. The [[decoder-only-stack|encoder half is gone]], and with it the block's third sublayer. Reaching back across [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|long distances]] happens inside this one triangle or not at all.

chapters.title: Where the Normalization Sits
chapters.body:
Neither sublayer replaces the vector. Each one computes a correction, and the correction is added back.

So a position's 768 numbers pass through the block along a straight path, with the attention result added at one point and the feed-forward result added at another. [[layer-normalization-gpt1|Layer normalization]] is applied around each of those two additions — though the paper never writes the block out. It says only that layernorm is used extensively throughout the model, and [[eq-decoder-stack|Equation 2]] compresses the whole thing into the word `transformer_block`.

Worth noticing what layer normalization normalizes over. It takes one position's 768 numbers, subtracts their mean, divides by their standard deviation, then applies a learned gain and a learned bias — 768 of each.

Which means it mixes nothing across positions either. Attention remains the only place in the block where one token's numbers touch another's.

[[dropout-gpt1|Dropout]] sits here too. The paper applies it at rate 0.1 on the [[residual-embedding-attention-dropout|residual branches and inside attention]]: the sublayer's contribution can be dropped, while the path carrying the input forward is left alone. A block with its branch fully dropped passes its input along unchanged.

The paper claims one concrete payoff for having layernorm everywhere. It says that presence is why a plain [[weight-initialization|$\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$ initialization]] was sufficient across all [[twelve-layer-depth|twelve blocks]] — an assertion made in the setup paragraph, with no ablation behind it.

chapters.title: One Map, Applied 512 Times
chapters.body:
The second sublayer has no index of position anywhere in it.

[[position-wise-feedforward-3072|It is two matrices]]: one taking 768 numbers up to 3072, one bringing 3072 back down to 768, with an [[gelu|activation]] between them. The same two matrices are used at position 1, at position 300 and at position 512.

So the sublayer does not see a sequence. It sees a batch of vectors and applies one function to each. Sequence length is irrelevant to it: doubling the context doubles the work and changes nothing else.

What that buys is a clean division of labour. Combining information across tokens happens in attention and only there. Turning a single token's current representation into something else — a nonlinear map through 3072 intermediate features, four times the width it started at — happens here and only here.

What it costs is that this sublayer cannot notice an arrangement. If a feature depends on two tokens standing in a particular relation, attention has to have already merged them into one vector before the feed-forward network can act on it.

Position never enters as an argument because it entered once as data. [[input-representation-h0|At layer zero]] a position embedding was added to the token embedding, so where a token sits is already part of the numbers being transformed.

The paper gives 3072 as a number in the setup and does not argue for it, nor for the 4:1 ratio it implies. Both arrive with the architecture, alongside the [[token-embedding-matrix|embedding matrix]] and the [[learned-position-embeddings|position table]] that feed it.

chapters.title: Twelve Rounds of the Same Two Steps
chapters.body:
Put the two sublayers back together and the block reads as a pair of alternating moves: gather from the past, then transform in place.

Run that twelve times and each round works on the output of the last. A token's vector after block four is not a token any more. It is whatever four rounds of gathering and transforming made of the prefix ending at that position. [[fig-1|Figure 1]] draws the pair once and marks it $\times 12$.

The paper does offer evidence that the rounds are not redundant. [[layers-transferred|Its layer-transfer analysis]] carries a varying number of pre-trained blocks into fine-tuning and reports that each added layer helps, up to 9% on MultiNLI for full transfer, which it reads as each layer holding functionality the target tasks can use. [[fig-2|Figure 2]] plots those curves.

That is a claim about the stack as a whole, not about either sublayer on its own. No experiment here isolates attention from the feed-forward network, varies the head count, or moves the 3072.

The closest thing to an architectural control is [[ablation-lstm-substitution|swapping the whole stack]] for a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM, which [[table-5|Table 5]] scores 5.6 average points worse. The paper's reading of that gap is offered as a hypothesis rather than a result: attention gives the model a [[transformer-inductive-bias|more structured memory]] than a recurrent state does.

Everything a target task will eventually see comes out of the top block, and [[final-token-activation|only at the last position]]. Twelve rounds have to have put it there.

n-the-scoreboard--the-margins--five-sour.title: Five Sources, Five Different Ceilings
n-the-scoreboard--the-margins--five-sour.intro: The parent named each dataset's source and left it there. This level takes them one at a time: what a caption, a government report or an exam question makes easy or hard, who actually held each column in Table 2, and how much of that column's margin is explained by the baseline rather than by the model.

chapters.title: Captions: Where Ensembling Is Worth More Than the Margin
chapters.body:
The paper gives [[snli]] one word of description: image captions. Follow what that word implies.

A caption is written to describe a picture. So the premise is one sentence, usually present tense, usually about objects and actions someone can see.

Nothing in it refers back to an earlier sentence, because there is no earlier sentence. That takes [[coreference]] almost entirely out of this column — one of the four phenomena the paper names when it says [[natural-language-inference]] is hard.

What is left is mostly lexical entailment. Does *person* follow from *man*, does *sleeping* rule out *running*. A caption corpus exercises that heavily and the rest of the list lightly.

Now the column itself in [[table-2]]. Two rows tie for the underlined previous best at 89.3: ESIM with [[elmo-deep-contextualized-word-representations|ELMo]] features as a five-model ensemble, and CAFE as a five-model ensemble.

CAFE also appears further down as a single model, scoring 88.5.

Subtract those two CAFE rows. Ensembling five separately trained copies of the same [[task-specific-architectures|task-built architecture]] buys 0.8 points on this column.

The paper's SNLI margin is 0.6.

So the [[absolute-improvement]] claimed here is smaller than what one baseline gained from ensembling alone. The single model at 89.9 is still ahead of both 89.3 rows, and the paper is entitled to the subtraction it makes.

But a like-for-like comparison — one model against one model — is 89.9 against CAFE's 88.5, a gap of 1.4. The paper never reports it that way, because its rule for [[baseline-comparisons]] is to take the best published number whatever produced it. On this column that rule works against the paper's own number, and on other columns it will work for it.

chapters.title: Three Genres, and What the Matched Gap Actually Measures
chapters.body:
[[multinli]]'s three named genres each stress something different.

Transcribed speech is disfluent. It has restarts, filler and sentences that never finish, so a system trained on clean text meets input it has not seen shaped that way.

Popular fiction is where cross-sentence reference finally appears: pronouns, characters named once and referred to afterwards. This is the source in the whole set that genuinely tests [[long-range-dependencies-gpt1|long-range reference]].

Government reports go the other way. Long formal clauses, nested qualifiers, and the syntactic ambiguity the paper lists as a difficulty.

The matched and mismatched development sets are the same task over different halves of that genre pool. So the difference between the two columns is meant to read as a transfer cost.

Walk it down the rows. CAFE's five-model ensemble loses 1.2 points crossing over, 80.2 to 79.0. The Stochastic Answer Network ensemble loses 0.5, 80.6 to 80.1. This paper's model loses 0.7, 82.1 to 81.4.

Then look at the two [[glue-benchmark]] multi-task rows. GenSen goes 71.4 to 71.3, and the multi-task [[lstm-gpt1|biLSTM]] with attention goes 72.2 to 72.1. Each loses 0.1.

Those are the smallest gaps in the column and they belong to the weakest systems, roughly ten points below everything else. A model that is not fitting the matched genres closely has little genre-specific fit to lose.

So the matched-minus-mismatched difference is not a clean measure of genre transfer. It is confounded with how well the system does at all.

MultiNLI is also the one NLI dataset doing double duty in this paper. Its development accuracy is what [[layers-transferred]] plots in the left panel of [[fig-2]], the sweep that reports up to 9 percent for transferring the full stack rather than the embeddings alone. That makes it the dataset the paper uses to argue about the [[task-agnostic-model]], not just to score it.

chapters.title: Science Exams and Wikipedia: The Emptiest Columns Give the Biggest Numbers
chapters.body:
[[scitail]] comes from science exam questions. That source is declarative and technical: statements about processes, with a vocabulary of terms that appear rarely in general text and almost no pronouns.

Whether stage one prepared the model for that vocabulary is not something the paper checks. [[bookscorpus]] is described only as over 7,000 unpublished books across genres, with no breakdown by subject, so how much science text the pre-trained weights ever saw is unknown.

The SciTail column holds exactly one baseline number: CAFE as a single model, 83.3. Not an ensemble — the previous best on this dataset was set by one run of one task-built system.

That same CAFE row scores 88.5 on SNLI. The architecture is 5.2 points lower on SciTail than on captions, which suggests the source is harder for it, or simply that fewer people had tuned against it.

The paper's 88.3 minus 83.3 gives the 5.0 the text quotes.

[[qnli]] is built over Wikipedia articles, and the paper says nothing more about its construction. Encyclopedia prose is well-formed and factual, which removes the disfluency problem, but its sentences carry dense entity reference.

Its column has two numbers. GenSen at 82.3 and the multi-task biLSTM with attention at 82.1 — 0.2 apart, both taken from the same GLUE paper, both systems spreading capacity across many tasks at once.

There is a way to measure how strong that ceiling is. GenSen, the row that sets it, scores 71.4 on matched MultiNLI, about nine points below the dedicated NLI systems in the same table.

So QNLI's previous best was held by a system that is off the pace on the one column where it can be compared directly. The 5.8 is real arithmetic, and it is also the thinnest contest in the table — worth holding in mind against the headline [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12]].

chapters.title: News, 2,490 Examples, and What Three Epochs Buys
chapters.body:
[[rte]] is drawn from news articles, which is the source in this set with the most cross-sentence reference and the densest named entities. On source alone it is the column closest to the phenomena the paper says make the task hard.

It is also the one the paper loses.

Start with the size ratio. SNLI's roughly 550,000 training pairs against RTE's 2,490 is a factor of about 220.

Now put that through the recipe. [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] fixes batch size 32, and [[three-epochs-fine-tuning|three epochs]] is reported as sufficient for most datasets.

On RTE, 2,490 examples at 32 per batch is about 78 updates per epoch. Three epochs is therefore roughly 230 gradient steps.

On SNLI the same settings give about 17,200 updates per epoch, so around 51,600 steps.

That is the concrete shape of the problem. The [[supervised-fine-tuning]] stage has two orders of magnitude less signal to work with on RTE than on SNLI, at the same learning rate of 6.25e-5 and the same [[classifier-dropout]].

The result is 56.0. Both GLUE multi-task rows sit above it: 61.7 takes the bold, and GenSen's 59.2 also clears it. The model is third of three here, not second — the table's only column where it is beaten twice.

The shortfall against the best is 61.7 minus 56.0, which is 5.7. That is almost exactly the size of the QNLI gain, 5.8, and it is measured against the same family of multi-task systems.

The paper's account is that RTE is small, and that multi-task training would likely help given how the model does on the larger NLI sets. It states plainly that it has not tried this.

So the explanation is a hypothesis about [[labeled-data-scarcity]] under the [[two-stage-training-procedure]], offered without a run behind it.

chapters.title: The Phenomenon List Against the Five Sources
chapters.body:
Line up the paper's own list of what makes inference hard — lexical entailment, coreference, lexical ambiguity, syntactic ambiguity — against where the sentences come from.

Lexical entailment is everywhere. Every one of the five requires deciding whether one word or phrase follows from another.

Coreference across sentences is thin. Captions have none by construction, exam statements have little, encyclopedia sentences some. It is really only fiction and transcribed speech inside MultiNLI, and news in RTE, that put it in front of the model.

Syntactic ambiguity concentrates in the same two places: government reports and news prose.

Now read the margins back against that. The two largest gains, 5.0 and 5.8, come from the columns whose sources exercise the least cross-sentence reference and whose baseline rows are thinnest. The two sources carrying the most of it return 1.5 and 1.3 on MultiNLI, and a 5.7-point loss on RTE.

That is a reading, not a finding, and the paper does not make it.

What the paper does claim from these five columns is an ability to reason over multiple sentences and to handle aspects of linguistic ambiguity. The support is aggregate accuracy on five datasets chosen for diverse sources. No error analysis by phenomenon is reported anywhere, so the list of four difficulties motivates the task and is never used to break down the result.

The diversity argument carries the weight instead: if one model leads on sources this different without being redesigned for any of them, that is the case for [[evaluation-task-families|breadth over depth]].

Direct evidence for cross-sentence reasoning sits elsewhere in the paper — in the reading-comprehension results the next chapters take up, and in the [[long-range-contiguous-text]] argument for the corpus. The parallel scoreboard outside inference is [[table-4]].

n-which-parts-do-the-work--three-removal.title: Four Columns Each Way, and a Weight Never Swept
n-which-parts-do-the-work--three-removal.intro: The parent gave the split and the arithmetic. This level goes into the cells themselves — what each column actually measures, which of the paper's two readings of the split survives contact with the numbers, what the weight $\lambda$ is doing mechanically at each setting, and which published numbers were produced by which of the two rows.

chapters.title: Two Rows, Eight Metrics
chapters.body:
The comparison needs both rows. The full model reads 45.4, 91.3, 82.3, 82.0, 70.3, 81.8, 88.1, 56.0, and averages 74.7. Set the [[ablation-no-auxiliary-objective]] row underneath it in [[table-5]] and every cell subtracts directly.

But the eight columns are not measured in one unit. The column headers mark the metric for each: [[cola]] is scored by Matthews correlation, [[mrpc]] and [[qqp]] by F1, [[sts-b]] by Pearson correlation, and [[sst-2]], [[multinli]], [[qnli]] and [[rte]] by accuracy.

So the 7.0 on one side and the 4.0 on the other are sums across a correlation coefficient, two F1 scores, a second correlation coefficient and four accuracies.

That is what the average column already does, and it is how the paper reports gains everywhere else as [[absolute-improvement]]. It is still worth saying plainly. A point of Matthews correlation on CoLA and a point of accuracy on RTE are not the same quantity, and the three tenths rests on adding them as if they were.

Now look at where the margins actually sit. Two of the eight pairs cancel exactly: 0.7 on SST-2 against 0.7 on MNLI, and 1.2 on STS-B against 1.2 on QNLI. Those four columns contribute nothing to the gap.

What is left is 2.5 on CoLA and 2.6 on MRPC against 0.5 on QQP and 1.6 on RTE. That is $5.1 - 2.1 = 3.0$, the whole difference.

The result turns on four cells, and the two largest single moves in the table both favour dropping the loss.

chapters.title: By Family, or By Size
chapters.body:
Section 5 says two things about this split, and they are not the same claim.

The first is by task family: the auxiliary objective helps on the NLI tasks and [[qqp]]. Three of Table 5's columns — [[multinli|MNLI]], QNLI and RTE — are [[natural-language-inference]] datasets, and QQP is named separately. That reading covers all four winning columns with no exception.

The second is the one the section leaves the reader with: the trend suggests larger datasets benefit and smaller ones do not. This is where RTE stops fitting, at 2490 training examples and the largest margin on its side.

There is a further gap. The paper never prints training-set sizes for these eight columns. [[table-1]] lists the twelve datasets by family and name, not by count.

Three sizes appear anywhere in the paper: RTE at 2490, [[sts-b]] at roughly 5.7k, and [[snli]] at roughly 550k. The size axis the trend is read along is asserted rather than shown.

And the ablation covers eight of the twelve datasets in [[evaluation-task-families]]. SNLI is not a column. Neither are [[scitail]], [[race-dataset]] or [[story-cloze-test]].

So the largest dataset the paper does size is absent from the table where size is invoked.

The hedge in "suggests" is the paper's own word, and it does not claim more than that. Read strictly, [[ablation-studies]] reports a family split cleanly and a size trend loosely.

chapters.title: One Weight, Two Settings
chapters.body:
What the removed term actually computes is worth unpacking before asking about its weight.

[[eq-combined-objective]] is $L_3(C) = L_2(C) + \lambda L_1(C)$. Both terms take $C$, the [[labeled-dataset-c]]. So [[auxiliary-lm-objective]] is not the pre-training loss over [[bookscorpus]] carried forward. It is next-token prediction run over the target task's own labelled inputs.

Those inputs are the sequences produced by [[task-specific-input-transformations]], markers and [[delimiter-token]] included. On an entailment task the model is predicting the next token of a premise-delimiter-hypothesis string.

That gives the amount of auxiliary signal a size: it scales with $|C|$. On RTE the term sees 2490 transformed pairs, and [[fine-tuning-hyperparameters]] runs only [[three-epochs-fine-tuning]] over them. On [[qqp]] it sees hundreds of thousands.

That is a mechanism the size trend could have been built on. The paper does not offer it, or any other.

[[auxiliary-objective-weight]] is one global constant, 0.5, across all twelve datasets. Nothing in the setup lets $\lambda$ vary by task, and the same [[fine-tuning-lr-and-batch]] settings are shared alongside it.

The ablation moves that one constant to 0. Two points, and they are the endpoints.

From two endpoints you cannot tell whether the average is monotone in $\lambda$ or dips between them. You also cannot tell whether the columns that lose at 0.5 would recover at 0.25 while the columns that win keep winning.

A quantity whose effect changes sign across columns is exactly the case where the size of the weight might matter per column, and that is the measurement not taken.

chapters.title: A Diagnostic on a Setting Already Spent
chapters.body:
The ordering is what makes this row different from the other two removals.

Every number in [[table-2]], [[table-3]] and [[table-4]] was produced at $\lambda = 0.5$. The scoreboard was fixed before the ablation asked whether 0.5 was the right value.

On four of the eight columns, that means the published figure is the lower of the two the paper measured.

[[cola]] is reported at 45.4 against a previous best of 35.0, and the section calls it an especially big jump. The row without the loss reads 47.9. SST-2 is reported at 91.3 and described as competitive with the state of the art rather than beating it; the other row reads 92.0. [[mrpc]] is 82.3 against 84.9. STS-B is reported as a 1 point absolute gain at 82.0, where the other row reads 83.2.

The paper does not go back and re-report any of these. The [[state-of-the-art-9-of-12]] count and the 72.8 on the [[glue-benchmark]] both stand on the $\lambda = 0.5$ run.

There is a defensible reason for that, though the paper does not state it. Picking the better of two settings per column would break the [[task-agnostic-model]] claim the whole [[two-stage-training-procedure]] is built to make: one recipe, unchanged, applied everywhere.

Leaving the headline numbers alone keeps that claim intact and makes four of them conservative — by accident of ordering, not by design.

What the row cannot be is a justification of 0.5. It measures a setting that had already been spent.
